lessons.title: 2.1.1 Keyboard
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

Functions must work using a keyboard interface without requiring precisely timed keystrokes. The limited exception concerns functions whose underlying operation genuinely depends on a movement path, not merely the way a developer chose to implement them.
Implementation and testing

Use native buttons and links and ensure custom controls respond to keyboard input. A signature-drawing function can depend on a path; entering text does not become path-dependent just because handwriting is offered. Test Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space and arrow keys where appropriate.
Real-world example: the barrier
A dashboard uses a div with an onclick handler for “Export”. It works with a mouse but is absent from the tab order. A keyboard user cannot download the report.
Improved design and verification
Use a native button with a click handler. Tab to it and activate it with Enter and Space. Then verify that the resulting download or dialog is available without a mouse.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
Export
Improved approach:
<button type="button" onclick="exportReport()">Export</button>
The native button is included in the keyboard focus order and supports standard activation. Check the exported result and any follow-up dialog too.
Detailed guidance

A keyboard interface is not limited to a physical keyboard. Switch devices, speech software and other assistive technologies may generate keyboard commands. When application functionality is wired only to mouse movement or pointer clicks, those users can be blocked even though the interface works on a touch screen. Begin testing at the browser address bar and navigate the whole task without touching the mouse, so an initial mouse click does not conceal an inaccessible starting point.

Native HTML controls provide a useful baseline: buttons participate in the normal tab order and implement familiar activation behavior. A link is appropriate for navigation; a button is appropriate for an action. Adding tabindex to a div only makes it focusable. It does not automatically provide the expected role, accessible name, keyboard behavior, disabled state or activation. If a complex custom widget is necessary, implement and test its complete interaction model rather than relying on focusability alone.

The path-dependent exception is narrower than a drag-and-drop implementation. Rearranging cards depends on the start and end positions, so a keyboard move command can perform the underlying task. Freehand drawing may require the movement path itself; evaluate the actual function rather than applying the exception to every drawing interface. The stricter AAA criterion 2.1.3 does not include that exception.

A useful test record includes the browser, operating system, starting focus, keys used, expected result and actual result. Exercise open and close controls, validation errors, dynamic results and dialog recovery. Check that focus remains visible under 2.4.7 and follows a meaningful sequence under 2.4.3; those are related criteria, not replacements for keyboard operability.
Further explanation and testing

A keyboard interface is a way of giving commands through keystrokes; the person may use a physical keyboard, a switch device that sends keyboard events, or another assistive technology. To assess an action, separate reaching its control from executing it and completing any resulting workflow. For instance, reaching an Export button is only the beginning if its file-format dialog, confirmation, or download control requires a mouse. A component that accepts focus but does not respond to an expected key is still a barrier.

Prefer the element that already expresses the intended operation: use a button to perform an action and a link to navigate. These elements supply useful browser behavior, but they do not fix a surrounding workflow automatically. For a custom composite widget, consult the interaction pattern appropriate to that widget and provide the expected movement and activation keys. Do not indiscriminately add every item to the tab order or intercept Tab when the page needs it for ordinary movement.

The path-dependent exception refers to the nature of the underlying function. Freehand painting depends on the path traced, whereas selecting a menu item does not. A control does not become exempt just because its author implemented selection through a gesture. During review, list each operation, the keystrokes used to reach and perform it, the resulting state, and any blocked step. Test in both directions and with no time pressure; do not confuse this baseline exception with the stricter AAA 2.1.3 requirement.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A sales chart has a button that opens a menu with “Download CSV” and “Download PDF.” Draw a table with one row per action: open menu, move between choices, activate a choice, and dismiss the menu. For each row, record focus position and the key used. If the menu opens on focus but cannot be closed, investigate 2.1.2 as well. If it can be closed but a choice only responds to mouse click, this keyboard criterion is still affected. Use a button for the menu trigger and ensure its expanded state reflects the visible menu; avoid using a clickable div as a shortcut to custom styling.
Implementation review

Implementation review: For an action, replace
Save
with and attach the same save operation to its click event. A native button provides keyboard focus and standard activation; do not add a second keydown handler that causes Enter or Space to save twice. Tab to the button, activate with Enter, then repeat with Space. Check the actual saved result, not merely whether the button receives focus. If save opens a confirmation, carry the keyboard test through confirmation and back to the form. For a link that navigates, use an anchor with a meaningful href rather than choosing a button merely because both can receive focus.
Worked example and edge cases

Consider a file manager where a pointer user can select a file, open its context menu, rename it, and confirm the new name. Follow that entire sequence using only a keyboard. A control can receive focus but still fail if its activation handler listens only for mouse events. Native buttons and links give a sound starting point, while custom composite controls also need the expected arrow-key behavior and clear instructions. After renaming, verify that the updated name is available and that focus has not disappeared. A drawing function may qualify for the path-dependent exception only when its underlying operation truly depends on the path; the exception does not cover unrelated controls such as saving, selecting a color, or opening a menu.
Planning a thorough review

Keyboard testing begins before the first page control. Place focus in the browser address bar, enter the page, and use Tab and Shift+Tab to trace the sequence. For native controls, exercise Enter and Space as appropriate; for a composite widget, check its documented arrow keys, selection behavior, and exit method. Record the control, the action attempted, the result, and the point where the task stopped. Repeat after opening any menu or dialog, because its interactive state may have a separate focus sequence. A focusable element is not necessarily operable, and a click handler is not evidence that keyboard activation works.

Look at the complete user journey as well as each control. A person who can select an item but cannot confirm or cancel it still cannot complete the task. Where scripts move focus, verify that focus lands on a meaningful, visible target and remains recoverable after closing a layer. Test with the browser's native keyboard behavior before adding custom handlers, and avoid overriding established keys without a clear reason. A keyboard-only check is valuable, but it does not replace examining pointer and assistive-technology behavior under the other applicable criteria.
Required practical activity
Navigate a menu and complete a form without touching a pointer. Record every action that cannot be reached or activated, then replace one clickable noninteractive element with a button.
Knowledge check
A custom menu opens only on mouse hover. What is the best correction?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

A user who moves focus into a component must be able to move away using the keyboard. An intentional focus loop inside a modal is not a trap if a keyboard user can close the modal and return to the page.
Implementation and testing
Provide conventional exit keys and a visible close control; if exiting requires an unusual method, explain it to the user. Test embedded widgets and dialogs as well as the surrounding page.
Real-world example: the barrier
A third-party date picker accepts keyboard focus but consumes every Tab and Escape key. Users cannot reach the rest of the form.
Improved design and verification
Provide a standard exit and verify focus can leave the widget. If an unusual key combination is unavoidable, explain it before the user enters.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A date picker intercepts Tab and Escape indefinitely.
Improved approach:
Escape closes the picker; Tab can move to the next form control.
A modal may contain focus while open if it provides an operable way to close it. Confirm that closing restores a useful focus position.
Detailed guidance

A keyboard trap is a focus situation from which a user cannot leave using a keyboard interface. It can isolate all later content on the page, so the impact is larger than a single broken control. Common causes include key handlers that cancel Tab, embedded widgets with incomplete keyboard support and dialogs whose close control cannot be reached or activated.

Do not confuse a temporary modal focus loop with an unavoidable trap. While a properly designed modal is open, keeping focus inside can prevent interaction with content behind it. The user must nevertheless have an operable route to close or otherwise leave the modal and continue the task. A visible close button in the focus order and a functioning Escape key are common choices, although the exact design depends on the component.

Test forward and backward movement using Tab and Shift+Tab. Try the documented close action, any conventional exit key and the control that originally opened the component. If leaving requires a method beyond standard unmodified arrow or Tab keys or other standard exit methods, tell users the method. Verify the instruction is available before the user becomes stuck.

After closing a modal, returning focus to its opener is often helpful because it preserves location. If the opener no longer exists, place focus at a logical replacement. Also test failure paths such as validation errors and third-party content; a successful exit from the happy path does not establish that every component is escapable.
Further explanation and testing

Focus indicates where keyboard input is directed. A trap occurs when a person can move into a component but cannot move away through a keyboard interface. The impact can extend beyond the component: the user may be unable to reach the form, browser controls, or other page content without abandoning or reloading the task. A focus loop inside a modal is different if the person can close the modal using the keyboard and continue afterward.

Test the entry, interaction, and exit of each component. Tab into a date picker, use its arrow keys to select a date, and then try Tab, Shift+Tab, Escape, and its close control as appropriate to the widget. If a nonstandard exit method is necessary, provide instructions before the user needs them. A visible Close button is useful only if focus can reach it and its keyboard activation works.

After closing a dialog, returning focus to the control that opened it often preserves the user’s context. If that control no longer exists, move focus to another logical location and explain the outcome where appropriate. Embedded content and third-party widgets deserve separate testing because their event handlers may consume keys differently from the host page. Record the exact keys and focus position when reporting a trap so a developer can reproduce it.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A date picker opens from a calendar button and moves focus to a date. Follow its normal keyboard instructions, then close it without selecting a date. The expected outcome is that the person can continue through the form. If Escape does nothing but a reachable Close button works, test that button before concluding a trap exists. If all keys are consumed and neither control can be reached, record the browser, entry point and key sequence. Restoring focus to the opener is often sensible, but if the opener has disappeared after selection choose another logical place rather than leaving focus nowhere.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Suppose a dialog intercepts Tab to keep focus inside while open. Test the first and last focusable controls in both directions, then use Escape or an operable Close button. A loop within an active dialog is not enough to prove a trap: the decisive question is whether the user can leave using the keyboard. If no standard exit is supported, instructions must describe the method needed to leave. After closing, check that focus returns to the opener or another meaningful position and that the next Tab reaches the surrounding task. Also test a nested embedded widget, whose key handling may prevent the dialog exit from working.
Worked example and edge cases

A calendar popup can appear to be a keyboard trap even when its initial controls are accessible. Enter the date field, open the calendar, move through the available dates, and attempt to leave without choosing one. If Escape closes the popup, check where focus lands and whether the next Tab moves on to the next field. If the interface uses a nonstandard exit mechanism, tell users what it is before they become stuck. A modal dialog may intentionally constrain focus to its controls while open, but it needs a keyboard-operable route out; a close button that can only be clicked does not solve the problem.
Planning a thorough review

Keyboard testing begins before the first page control. Place focus in the browser address bar, enter the page, and use Tab and Shift+Tab to trace the sequence. For native controls, exercise Enter and Space as appropriate; for a composite widget, check its documented arrow keys, selection behavior, and exit method. Record the control, the action attempted, the result, and the point where the task stopped. Repeat after opening any menu or dialog, because its interactive state may have a separate focus sequence. A focusable element is not necessarily operable, and a click handler is not evidence that keyboard activation works.

Look at the complete user journey as well as each control. A person who can select an item but cannot confirm or cancel it still cannot complete the task. Where scripts move focus, verify that focus lands on a meaningful, visible target and remains recoverable after closing a layer. Test with the browser's native keyboard behavior before adding custom handlers, and avoid overriding established keys without a clear reason. A keyboard-only check is valuable, but it does not replace examining pointer and assistive-technology behavior under the other applicable criteria.
Required practical activity
Open a dialog using only the keyboard, close it, and continue to the next page control. Document where focus goes after closing.
Knowledge check
A dialog cycles focus internally but Escape and its Close button both work. What should you test next?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.1.3 Keyboard (No Exception)
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.1.3 Keyboard (No Exception) (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.1.3 Keyboard (No Exception) (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

This AAA criterion requires all functionality to be keyboard-operable without timing-dependent keystrokes and does not include the path-dependent exception in 2.1.1. It sets a higher target than the Level A baseline.
Implementation and testing

Design alternative workflows for tasks that normally use pointer paths; a drawing application might provide controls for creating and editing shapes by coordinates. Whether an alternative provides the same functionality requires careful evaluation.
Real-world example: the barrier
A diagram editor offers only freehand pointer drawing, so a person who relies on keyboard input cannot create the same diagram.
Improved design and verification
Provide keyboard-accessible shape insertion, movement and editing. Evaluate whether these controls actually cover every supported operation rather than only basic navigation.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A drawing tool supports adding and moving shapes only by dragging.
Improved approach:
Keyboard controls insert shapes, set coordinates and dimensions, and confirm placement.
Keyboard alternatives must offer all the underlying functionality. A menu that only selects a shape without allowing placement does not complete the workflow.
Detailed guidance

Level A keyboard support has an exception for functions where the underlying operation genuinely depends on the path of movement. This AAA criterion removes that exception. A gesture used as a convenient input method should not be confused with a function that is intrinsically path-dependent: sorting cards, for example, has identifiable start and end positions.

For a graphic editor, list each operation rather than checking only whether menus open: create a shape, select it, move it, adjust dimensions and rotation, edit its properties and delete it. A keyboard interface might use numeric fields, selection controls and commands. Check that those controls can produce the same outcomes, not just approximate a subset.

Test without relying on timed key sequences. Document whether every action is achievable and whether the user receives appropriate feedback. This AAA target may require substantial design work for freehand or path-based activities; avoid claiming full coverage merely because a few keyboard shortcuts exist.
Worked verification

In a diagram editor, list every available operation before testing: creating an object, changing its shape, positioning it, editing its label, and deleting it. Try each operation with the keyboard. A keyboard-accessible toolbar is insufficient if the only way to place the selected object is to trace a pointer path. Record missing operations separately from focus problems, because reaching a control does not prove the whole task can be completed.
Further explanation and testing

The enhanced keyboard criterion asks for every function to be operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timing for individual keystrokes. Unlike the Level A keyboard criterion, it has no exception for an operation whose underlying function depends on a movement path. The difference matters when evaluating a drawing, handwriting, or mapping tool: basic keyboard navigation does not establish that all its functions are available.

Start by inventorying what a pointer user can actually do, including setting coordinates, modifying shapes, deleting elements, and confirming the result. For each operation, design and test an equivalent keyboard workflow. A shape-placement dialog could expose position and size fields and a confirmation button. Check whether it supports the same meaningful operations rather than merely offering an alternative that changes the task.

Test without precisely timed keystrokes. A person should not have to press two keys within a narrow interval merely to complete a normal operation. Verify key instructions, focus location, error recovery, and the final result. If freehand drawing produces unique paths that the keyboard workflow cannot create, document the gap rather than claiming conformance based on a partial alternative.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Compare a pointer-operated map editor with its proposed keyboard alternative. If the pointer lets a user draw an arbitrary boundary but the keyboard interface only selects from three predefined shapes, the alternative does not cover the same capability. A coordinate editor might support editing each boundary point, but it must also support creating and removing points and confirming the result. Test long key sequences at a deliberate pace; a shortcut that requires rapid repeated presses is not a substitute for operations that can be invoked without that timing.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A canvas diagram tool exposes Insert rectangle, X position, Y position, width, height, and Delete as keyboard controls. Walk through creation, modification, and deletion without a pointer. Then compare with the pointer feature set: if users can draw arbitrary curves but keyboard users can only insert rectangles, the coverage is incomplete. The stronger criterion has no path-dependent exception, so record unsupported curve operations rather than assuming the baseline exception carries over. Check that every coordinate field is labeled and that error correction does not require rapid key sequences. A visible toolbar and focusable canvas alone do not demonstrate equivalent functionality.
Worked example and edge cases

Imagine a diagram editor where creating a connection requires dragging a line from one node to another. A keyboard alternative could let a user select the source node, choose an add-connection command, select the destination, and edit the resulting line. Evaluate more than initial creation: users may also need to move endpoints, change labels, remove connections, and save the diagram. This enhanced criterion removes the path-dependent exception in the Level A keyboard criterion. Do not infer that a simple keyboard shortcut for opening the editor covers the drawing operations themselves. Check the complete set of functions and compare their results across input methods.
Planning a thorough review

Keyboard testing begins before the first page control. Place focus in the browser address bar, enter the page, and use Tab and Shift+Tab to trace the sequence. For native controls, exercise Enter and Space as appropriate; for a composite widget, check its documented arrow keys, selection behavior, and exit method. Record the control, the action attempted, the result, and the point where the task stopped. Repeat after opening any menu or dialog, because its interactive state may have a separate focus sequence. A focusable element is not necessarily operable, and a click handler is not evidence that keyboard activation works.

Look at the complete user journey as well as each control. A person who can select an item but cannot confirm or cancel it still cannot complete the task. Where scripts move focus, verify that focus lands on a meaningful, visible target and remains recoverable after closing a layer. Test with the browser's native keyboard behavior before adding custom handlers, and avoid overriding established keys without a clear reason. A keyboard-only check is valuable, but it does not replace examining pointer and assistive-technology behavior under the other applicable criteria.
Required practical activity
Choose a drawing or map interface and outline a keyboard workflow for each operation, including moving, resizing, and confirming an object.
Knowledge check
What distinguishes this AAA criterion from 2.1.1?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Single-character shortcuts can fire accidentally when a speech user dictates text or when focus is unexpected. Shortcuts made solely from letters, punctuation, numbers or symbols need a safeguard.
Implementation and testing
Provide a way to turn the shortcut off, remap it to include a non-printable modifier, or activate it only while the relevant component has focus. Verify these options work after settings are saved.
Real-world example: the barrier
In a video page the global “m” shortcut mutes audio while a speech user dictates an unrelated message. The action is unexpected and interrupts the task.
Improved design and verification
Offer a setting to disable or remap the character shortcut, or limit it to focus on the video component. Test typing and dictation outside that component.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
document.addEventListener("keydown", e => { if (e.key === "m") mute(); });
Improved approach:
Enable the character shortcut only when the player has focus, or offer disable/remap settings.
A global character handler can activate while someone dictates or types. Check inputs and focus changes, including settings persistence.
Detailed guidance

A character key shortcut consists only of printable letters, numbers, punctuation or symbols. Speech input can accidentally trigger it when dictated words are interpreted as commands; a keyboard user may also activate it while typing if the page handles keystrokes globally.

Three safeguards are available: allow users to turn the shortcut off, let them remap it to include a non-printable modifier such as Ctrl or Alt, or make the shortcut active only while the relevant component has focus. A shortcut limited to a focused component must actually remain inactive outside that focus context.

Test a shortcut while a text field is focused and while focus is elsewhere. If remapping is provided, check for conflicts, communicate the new combination and verify it persists as intended. Do not silently suppress ordinary typing or rely on a user remembering to avoid a particular character.
Worked verification

Test a shortcut in three contexts: the intended component has focus, a text field has focus, and focus is elsewhere on the page. A shortcut limited to the component should activate only in the first case. If a preference disables or remaps it, reload the application and check whether the preference is retained. Also verify that the revised shortcut does not interfere with typing or another essential command.
Further explanation and testing

A character key shortcut is triggered by one or more printable characters without a non-printable modifier. It can be useful for rapid navigation, but speech recognition may interpret a dictated character as a command, and a keyboard user may press it while focus is in an unexpected location. The criterion offers safeguards: turn the shortcut off, remap it to include a non-printable modifier, or make it active only when its component has focus.

Consider a video player that uses the letter m for mute. One repair is a preference that disables the shortcut. Another is remapping it to a combination with a modifier; another is limiting the shortcut to the focused player component. Make the chosen mechanism discoverable and operable without triggering the unwanted command. Ensure that an input field elsewhere on the page can receive the letter normally.

Try the shortcut with focus on the player, a neighboring search field, and another page control. If the user disables or changes it, repeat the test after navigating away and returning according to the product’s stated settings behavior. Do not treat a note in documentation as a substitute for one of the specified safeguards. Also check that the new shortcut does not interfere with common browser or assistive technology commands.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A course player uses “k” to pause while a learner writes notes in a separate text field. First test with the player focused, then type “k” into the notes field. If the player pauses while notes are being entered, the shortcut is active too broadly unless another allowed safeguard is in place. Add a disable option, modifier-based remapping, or focus limitation, then retest. Document the chosen safeguard in the product’s keyboard-shortcut help, but remember that the safeguard itself must work; documentation alone does not stop accidental activation.
Implementation review

Implementation review: In a media component, a keydown listener for m can check whether the relevant player has focus before toggling mute. Alternatively, settings can disable the character shortcut or remap it with a non-printable modifier. Open a separate text field and type the character: audio should not change when the focus-based safeguard is used. Test the focused player as well, so the repair does not inadvertently remove intended behavior. If a setting is offered, use the control itself with keyboard input and verify its saved state as promised by the product. A help page explaining the shortcut is not one of the required safeguards.
Worked example and edge cases

A video player uses the letter M to mute sound. If the shortcut is registered on the entire document, it may fire when a person dictates a sentence or types into a nearby comment field. Choose one of the permitted safeguards: disable the shortcut, allow the user to remap it with a non-printable modifier, or make it active only when the relevant component has focus. Test the chosen safeguard after moving focus away, typing in a field, and returning to the player. If a preference is offered, verify that the saved setting is applied consistently on the next visit rather than just changing the appearance of a switch.
Planning a thorough review

Keyboard testing begins before the first page control. Place focus in the browser address bar, enter the page, and use Tab and Shift+Tab to trace the sequence. For native controls, exercise Enter and Space as appropriate; for a composite widget, check its documented arrow keys, selection behavior, and exit method. Record the control, the action attempted, the result, and the point where the task stopped. Repeat after opening any menu or dialog, because its interactive state may have a separate focus sequence. A focusable element is not necessarily operable, and a click handler is not evidence that keyboard activation works.

Look at the complete user journey as well as each control. A person who can select an item but cannot confirm or cancel it still cannot complete the task. Where scripts move focus, verify that focus lands on a meaningful, visible target and remains recoverable after closing a layer. Test with the browser's native keyboard behavior before adding custom handlers, and avoid overriding established keys without a clear reason. A keyboard-only check is valuable, but it does not replace examining pointer and assistive-technology behavior under the other applicable criteria.
Required practical activity
Find a single-letter shortcut in a mock editor. Design and test one of the three allowed safeguards.
Knowledge check
A site assigns the letter s as a global shortcut. Which safeguard is appropriate?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

Content-imposed time limits can prevent people from reading, using assistive technology, or recovering from interruptions. Users need control over qualifying time limits, subject to defined exceptions.
Implementation and testing

Offer a way to turn the limit off, adjust it to at least ten times the default, or warn before expiry and allow at least 20 seconds for a simple extension, at least ten times. Real-time, essential and longer-than-20-hour exceptions have specific conditions; do not assume every security timeout is automatically exempt.
Real-world example: the barrier
A registration form signs a user out five minutes after loading without warning and discards partially entered answers.
Improved design and verification
Before expiry offer a simple extension with at least 20 seconds to respond, repeatable at least ten times, or use another permitted option. Determine whether any claimed exception genuinely applies.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A checkout expires after five minutes without warning.
Improved approach:
Warn before expiration and let users extend with one action within at least 20 seconds; allow at least ten extensions.
An extension is only one option: turning the limit off or adjusting it sufficiently may also satisfy the criterion. Evaluate exceptions carefully.
Detailed guidance

Time limits may be explicit, like a visible countdown, or implicit, like a session that expires while the user fills in a form. Reading with a screen reader, using a switch device, translating instructions or recovering from an interruption can all lengthen a task. A warning that appears after data is discarded cannot give the person time to respond.

The criterion specifies multiple permitted approaches. An interface can let a user turn off the limit before encountering it, adjust it over a range at least ten times the default, or provide a warning with at least 20 seconds for a simple action to extend the limit at least ten times. These are alternatives; a design need not implement all three, but it must meet all conditions of whichever option it relies on.

A real-time exception applies where the time limit is a required part of a real-time event and no alternative is possible. The essential exception requires that extending the limit invalidate the activity. A time limit longer than 20 hours has its own exception. Do not treat a commercial preference or a security concern as proof that an exception automatically applies; examine the exact situation and documented requirement.

For a test, use a short configurable timeout in a development environment. Enter data, wait for the warning and check that the extension action is simple and keyboard operable. Measure the available response time and repeat the extension at least ten times. Confirm that the pending data survives each extension and investigate interactions with authentication or server-side expiry.
Further explanation and testing

A time limit imposed by content can affect someone who reads slowly, uses a screen reader, needs a break, or navigates through many fields with a switch. The practical problem is not the presence of a clock by itself: it is that the task, session, or opportunity ends before the person can complete it. Identify each deadline separately, including form expiry, quiz deadlines, temporary verification codes, and automatically refreshed content.

The criterion offers alternatives with precise conditions. A user can turn off the limit before encountering it, adjust it before encountering it to at least ten times the default, or receive a warning before expiry that provides at least 20 seconds for a simple extension and permits at least ten extensions. The applicable exceptions have their own conditions, including real-time, essential, and longer-than-20-hour situations. A preferred business rule is not automatically essential.

For an extension design, start a test session with a shortened but representative timeout. Record when the warning appears, whether focus remains manageable, and whether one simple action extends the same session. Repeat the extension at least ten times and check that entered data stays intact. Test the turn-off or adjustment path before starting the timed activity if the product chooses one of those alternatives. Separately evaluate reauthentication and data-loss requirements when expiry can still occur.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A five-minute application session offers a warning ten seconds before expiry and one extension. This does not satisfy the specified warning-and-extension option: the user must have at least 20 seconds to extend with a simple action, and the extension must be available at least ten times. The team could instead satisfy another allowed option, such as allowing the limit to be turned off before it is encountered. Check whether session expiry actually ends the activity and whether an exception truly applies. Also test that the warning can be perceived and its extension control operated with the user’s input method.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A form expires after five minutes. A warning appears at four minutes forty seconds and provides an Extend button. Time the interval in the actual application: it must provide at least 20 seconds to respond for this option, use a simple action, and allow at least ten extensions. A warning shown after expiry cannot provide that opportunity. If the application instead permits turning the limit off or adjusting it to at least ten times the default before it is encountered, test that chosen path. Preserve sample answers while testing and document whether the real-time, essential, or longer-than-20-hour exception actually applies.
Worked example and edge cases

A checkout reserves a basket for five minutes. A warning that appears only five seconds before expiry does not provide the specified warning-and-extension option, even if the Extend button works. With that option, give at least twenty seconds to act and permit extension at least ten times; test each extension and confirm that the contents of the basket remain available. Turning the limit off or permitting adjustment to at least ten times the default are other options. Assess the particular exception before relying on it. A desire to keep sessions short is not by itself proof that a time limit is essential or that the activity is a real-time event.
Planning a thorough review

When a feature depends on time, map the point at which a timer starts, the event that ends it, and the consequence for the user's task. Read the interface copy and then observe the actual server behavior; a visible countdown can differ from the expiration enforced on the server. Check what happens to entered information before expiry, at expiry, and after a return to the task. Use a test account and sample data so that losing a draft does not affect a real user. If an extension or preference is offered, check its actual effect and whether it remains understandable and operable with a keyboard.

Different timing criteria protect different outcomes. A warning about data loss is not necessarily a way to extend a time limit; a pause for moving content is not necessarily a way to resume an expired session. Apply the conditions and exceptions of the specific criterion in the lesson, rather than treating every timer as the same case. For any exception, describe the real function and why the conditions apply. Product convenience, advertising schedules, or a general preference for short sessions are not automatically proof that a time limit or interruption is essential.
Required practical activity
Review a checkout timeout. Specify warning timing, extension control, repeat count and a test that preserves entered data.
Knowledge check
Which warning-and-extension design meets the specified timing option?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

Automatically moving, blinking or scrolling information running for more than five seconds alongside other content needs a pause, stop or hide mechanism unless essential. Automatically updating information alongside other content also needs control, without the five-second condition.
Implementation and testing
Provide a keyboard-operable pause or frequency control near the content. A motion control is not a substitute for evaluating flashing under 2.3.
Real-world example: the barrier
An automatic carousel continually changes next to a sign-up form, while a nearby stock ticker refreshes on its own. The movement and updates interrupt reading.
Improved design and verification
Give users a pause control for the carousel and a pause or update-frequency control for the ticker. Test with keyboard and check the controls affect the actual content.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
setInterval(nextSlide, 3000) runs with no user control.
Improved approach:
Provide a Pause button that stops automatic movement; resume only when requested.
For auto-updating content, provide pause, stop, hide or update-frequency control. Test that controls do not merely hide the animation button.
Detailed guidance

Motion and automatically changing content can compete for attention or prevent users from reading at their own pace. The criterion addresses two cases with different conditions. Automatically moving, blinking or scrolling content presented alongside other content needs a control when it lasts more than five seconds, unless the motion is essential. Automatically updating content presented alongside other content also needs a control, but the five-second condition does not apply to that case.

The offered mechanism can pause, stop or hide qualifying movement. For auto-updates, controlling the update frequency is another option. Place the control where users can find and operate it without having to chase the moving item; give it a meaningful label and ensure its state matches what it does.

A pause may not need to replay every update that occurred while the content was paused; in a live stream that may not be technically possible or may be misleading. Test that the pause genuinely stops the relevant change, that the rest of the page remains usable and that the chosen behavior makes sense when updates resume.
Worked verification

Do not confuse stopping an animation with stopping changing information. For a carousel, pause movement and verify the current slide stays still. For a live feed, record its contents, pause updates, wait through at least one update interval, and check that new items do not interrupt reading. If updates resume, explain whether the feed catches up or starts from the latest state so users can make an informed choice.
Further explanation and testing

Moving or updating content competes with a reader’s attention and can make a piece of information disappear before it has been understood. This includes automatic carousels, scrolling announcements, animated content, and live feeds. The criterion distinguishes movement, blinking, or scrolling from auto-updating information, and their conditions are not identical.

For moving, blinking, or scrolling information, examine whether it starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds, and is presented alongside other content. If so, provide a pause, stop, or hide mechanism unless the movement is essential. For auto-updating information that starts automatically and is presented alongside other content, offer pause, stop, hide, or control of update frequency unless essential; the five-second condition does not apply in the same way.

An operable control must change the actual behavior, not merely remove the Pause button. Test by pausing a carousel and waiting longer than its slide interval. For a live feed, verify that updates stop interrupting the displayed information, and make it clear what happens when updates resume. Place controls where users can find and use them with a keyboard. Evaluate seizure-related flashing separately because a pause control does not automatically satisfy flash restrictions.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A carousel automatically advances every four seconds and sits beside an application form. Add a Pause control, activate it, and wait longer than two slide intervals. The content should stay still until the user chooses otherwise. Next inspect a nearby live feed that changes automatically: a motion-pause button for the carousel does not control feed updates. The feed needs its own suitable pause, stop, hide, or frequency control when the criterion applies. Neither control makes a rapidly flashing animation safe; inspect flashing under the seizure criteria separately.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A carousel advances on a timer. Its Pause button should stop the timer or otherwise stop the actual movement, update its own label or state appropriately, and remain keyboard operable. Activate Pause and observe for longer than the normal interval; merely hiding the slide does not show the motion has stopped. A live feed next to the carousel is a separate auto-updating item and needs an appropriate control if the criterion applies. Test each source independently. Do not apply the carousel’s five-second condition to conclude that a rapidly updating feed needs no user control.
Worked example and edge cases

A dashboard contains a rotating promotion and a live score feed. Treat these as separate behaviors. Automatic movement, blinking, or scrolling that starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds, and appears alongside other content requires a pause, stop, or hide mechanism unless essential. Automatically updating information presented alongside other content also needs the specified controls, without applying that five-second rule. Test whether Pause actually stops updates rather than merely freezing an animation while content continues to change underneath. The control must be reachable and usable; check keyboard operation and verify that restarting updates does not erase the user's current context.
Planning a thorough review

When a feature depends on time, map the point at which a timer starts, the event that ends it, and the consequence for the user's task. Read the interface copy and then observe the actual server behavior; a visible countdown can differ from the expiration enforced on the server. Check what happens to entered information before expiry, at expiry, and after a return to the task. Use a test account and sample data so that losing a draft does not affect a real user. If an extension or preference is offered, check its actual effect and whether it remains understandable and operable with a keyboard.

Different timing criteria protect different outcomes. A warning about data loss is not necessarily a way to extend a time limit; a pause for moving content is not necessarily a way to resume an expired session. Apply the conditions and exceptions of the specific criterion in the lesson, rather than treating every timer as the same case. For any exception, describe the real function and why the conditions apply. Product convenience, advertising schedules, or a general preference for short sessions are not automatically proof that a time limit or interruption is essential.
Required practical activity
Inspect an automatic carousel and a live news feed. Determine which controls each needs and verify the controls remain available by keyboard.
Knowledge check

Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.2.3 No Timing
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.2.3 No Timing (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.2.3 No Timing (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
At AAA, timing is not an essential part of the activity, except for non-interactive synchronized media and real-time events. This is stronger than merely offering an extension under 2.2.1.
Implementation and testing

For self-paced quizzes, separate elapsed-time information from the ability to answer. Retain meaningful exceptions for genuinely real-time events rather than treating business preference as a technical necessity.
Real-world example: the barrier
A self-paced practice assessment requires every answer within thirty seconds, although its purpose is learning rather than a live contest.
Improved design and verification
Remove the countdown as a condition of completion. If displaying elapsed time is useful, ensure it does not end the activity or prevent answering.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A practice form expires after 60 seconds.
Improved approach:
Allow learners to submit at their own pace.
A timer may be displayed as information, but it must not be essential to completing the activity except within the specified exceptions.
Detailed guidance

This AAA criterion addresses whether timing is essential to an activity. It is stronger than 2.2.1, which permits specific adjustment or extension mechanisms. A learner might still feel pressured by a countdown even if several extensions are available.

For a practice task, allow the learner to read, think and answer without a deadline determining success. If timing is used for analysis, consider showing elapsed time while preserving the ability to complete the task at any pace. Timing is not automatically essential just because the original design included a timer.

The criterion specifies exceptions for non-interactive synchronized media and real-time events. An actual live auction is different from a recorded tutorial or self-paced form. Review the underlying activity, identify whether the exception applies, and test the entire task without a deadline.
Worked verification

Distinguish a deadline that controls task completion from a clock displayed for reference. A self-study exercise can show elapsed time while still accepting answers indefinitely. Test by leaving it idle beyond the former deadline, returning, changing an answer, and submitting. A live event may involve timing that is inherent to its real-world operation; the fact that a product owner prefers a deadline does not by itself make timing essential.
Further explanation and testing

The enhanced timing criterion removes timing as an essential part of the activity except for the stated cases, including non-interactive synchronized media and real-time events. It provides a stronger target than allowing a user to extend an otherwise compulsory deadline. A person working through an ordinary self-paced lesson should be able to pause, consult a resource, and return without losing the chance to complete the activity.

For a practice assessment, separate a timer used for feedback from a deadline that ends the attempt. Showing elapsed time may be useful if it does not block submission or make speed a condition of success. If the task is a genuinely real-time event, identify the reason timing is inherent in the activity rather than citing convenience or a general preference for shorter sessions.

Try beginning the assessment, leaving it idle beyond the previous timeout, returning, editing an answer, and submitting. Verify that a hidden server-side expiration does not negate the visible change. Also check reauthentication and draft preservation where a session may expire independently of the activity. A warning or one extra minute may improve an experience but does not by itself remove timing as an essential part of the task.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A training quiz awards a score only if the learner submits within two minutes. A ten-minute extension helps but still makes time a condition of completing the ordinary self-paced activity. Remove that condition and preserve answers while the learner reads or takes a break. A visible elapsed-time display may remain if it is informative and does not terminate the task. If a session security timeout still exists, test that reauthentication and restored answers allow the learner to resume. Evaluate whether any claimed real-time exception applies to this specific task.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A practice quiz originally rejects submissions after 60 seconds. Remove that server-side rejection as well as the visual countdown so users can finish at their own pace. Retaining an elapsed-time display for self-reflection is different from requiring a submission deadline. Test by pausing longer than the original limit and submitting a changed answer. If authentication expires, check that sign-in and restored data still permit completion. An extension that remains compulsory improves the experience but does not remove timing as an essential part of an ordinary self-paced activity.
Worked example and edge cases

A practice exam displays elapsed time for the learner's own reference but never ends the attempt because of a countdown. That is different from adding a ten-minute extension to a deadline: this enhanced criterion removes timing as an essential part of the activity, subject to its stated exceptions. When reviewing a self-paced exercise, inspect server-side expiration as well as the visible timer. A hidden submission deadline can still prevent completion. Record what happens when the learner pauses for a long interval, returns, edits an answer, and submits. Do not treat a live auction's genuinely real-time nature as evidence that an ordinary practice form must also be timed.
Planning a thorough review

When a feature depends on time, map the point at which a timer starts, the event that ends it, and the consequence for the user's task. Read the interface copy and then observe the actual server behavior; a visible countdown can differ from the expiration enforced on the server. Check what happens to entered information before expiry, at expiry, and after a return to the task. Use a test account and sample data so that losing a draft does not affect a real user. If an extension or preference is offered, check its actual effect and whether it remains understandable and operable with a keyboard.

Different timing criteria protect different outcomes. A warning about data loss is not necessarily a way to extend a time limit; a pause for moving content is not necessarily a way to resume an expired session. Apply the conditions and exceptions of the specific criterion in the lesson, rather than treating every timer as the same case. For any exception, describe the real function and why the conditions apply. Product convenience, advertising schedules, or a general preference for short sessions are not automatically proof that a time limit or interruption is essential.
Required practical activity

Knowledge check

Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.2.4 Interruptions
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.2.4 Interruptions (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.2.4 Interruptions (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Interruptions can disrupt concentration and assistive technology output. The AAA requirement lets users postpone or suppress interruptions except those involving an emergency.
Implementation and testing
Make non-emergency notifications configurable and avoid shifting focus to a promotion while a person is typing. Explain what has been suppressed and let the user retrieve it later.
Real-world example: the barrier
A promotional dialog appears while a learner is completing a difficult form and moves keyboard focus away from the current field.
Improved design and verification
Allow the learner to defer or suppress this non-emergency interruption and retrieve the message later. Do not suppress emergency warnings under this exception.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A promotion opens a modal and steals focus during form entry.
Improved approach:
Offer notification preferences or postpone a non-emergency message until requested.
Check that deferred notifications are retrievable and that emergency alerts remain handled appropriately.
Detailed guidance

An interruption redirects attention away from the user’s chosen task. A pop-up promotion, automatic chat invitation or forced update can interrupt a screen reader announcement or break concentration during a complex form. A message the user explicitly opened is different from an unsolicited interruption.

Give users control to postpone or suppress non-emergency interruptions. Preferences might include a quiet mode, a notification center or a deferred prompt. Do not move keyboard focus to a non-emergency message while the person is typing, and provide a reasonable way to find postponed information when it is relevant.

Emergency interruptions are an exception. Test by starting a form, triggering ordinary notifications and checking that the user can defer or prevent them while continuing the same task. Verify that the setting affects the actual interruption rather than only muting a sound.
Worked verification

Interruptions include more than dialog boxes: sounds, banners, and notifications can divert attention while someone reads or types. Offer a preference to postpone or suppress non-emergency interruptions, and verify it with an interruption triggered during a task. Check that the current focus and entered text remain intact and that the user can later find deferred information. Keep emergency messages distinguishable from ordinary promotions.
Further explanation and testing

An interruption is information or an event that diverts the user from their current activity. Unexpected promotional dialogs, chat invitations, and repeated notification sounds can disrupt concentration or cut across assistive technology output. This enhanced criterion requires a way to postpone or suppress interruptions, except interruptions involving an emergency.

A notification setting might let the user turn off promotional prompts or postpone them until the current task is complete. Avoid moving focus to a non-emergency modal while someone is entering data. If the message contains information the person may need later, provide a place to retrieve it rather than silently discarding it. Emergency alerts are treated differently under the criterion, so distinguish their purpose and urgency from ordinary product announcements.

While completing a form, trigger each configured interruption and observe whether focus, typed text, and progress remain stable. Repeat after choosing the postponement or suppression setting. Check the setting with keyboard and screen reader input and confirm that notifications follow the user’s choice. Evaluate visual interruptions and sounds, not only the largest dialog in the design.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A product shows a sales offer in a modal while the user types an application. Offer a setting to suppress promotions or postpone the message, then trigger the offer while the user is in the middle of a field. Verify that the typed value and focus stay intact and that the choice can be changed later. A genuine emergency warning is treated differently, so the product should not place ordinary marketing messages into the emergency category. The test should include audible as well as visual notifications if both can interrupt the task.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A notification preference can suppress promotional popups while a person fills in a form. Trigger the promotion while focus is in a text field and verify that no modal steals focus when suppression is enabled. If postponement is offered, verify the notification can be found later and that the user can change the preference. Test nonvisual interruptions such as notification sounds as well as modal dialogs. An emergency alert is handled by the exception; the team should not classify routine advertising as an emergency merely to bypass a user preference.
Worked example and edge cases

During a job application, a non-emergency chat invitation opens a modal and interrupts typing. A useful preference lets the applicant suppress or postpone such invitations while retaining a way to review them later. Test both choices: with suppression enabled, the invitation should not seize focus or interrupt the task; with postponement selected, it should be delivered at the chosen time. Emergency interruptions are treated differently under this criterion, so classify the actual message rather than assuming that every notification is urgent. Verify that the setting covers notifications emitted by embedded services as well as those produced by the application itself.
Planning a thorough review

When a feature depends on time, map the point at which a timer starts, the event that ends it, and the consequence for the user's task. Read the interface copy and then observe the actual server behavior; a visible countdown can differ from the expiration enforced on the server. Check what happens to entered information before expiry, at expiry, and after a return to the task. Use a test account and sample data so that losing a draft does not affect a real user. If an extension or preference is offered, check its actual effect and whether it remains understandable and operable with a keyboard.

Different timing criteria protect different outcomes. A warning about data loss is not necessarily a way to extend a time limit; a pause for moving content is not necessarily a way to resume an expired session. Apply the conditions and exceptions of the specific criterion in the lesson, rather than treating every timer as the same case. For any exception, describe the real function and why the conditions apply. Product convenience, advertising schedules, or a general preference for short sessions are not automatically proof that a time limit or interruption is essential.
Required practical activity
Classify a promotional banner, a chat invitation and an emergency alert. Design controls for the non-emergency interruptions.
Knowledge check

Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.2.5 Re-authenticating
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.2.5 Re-authenticating (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.2.5 Re-authenticating (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

If an authenticated session expires, users need to re-authenticate and continue their activity without losing data. Losing an unfinished application can be especially costly for users who need more time.
Implementation and testing
Preserve the in-progress state securely, return to the same step after login, and avoid submitting on the user’s behalf. Consider shared devices, retention policies and privacy when choosing storage.
Real-world example: the barrier
A session expires while an applicant is halfway through a long application. After signing in again, the application is blank.
Improved design and verification
Preserve the in-progress state securely and restore the same task after successful authentication. Test the expiry and re-entry path without automatically submitting.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
Session expiry clears all unsaved form fields.
Improved approach:
Save the draft safely, request sign-in, then restore the same task and data.
Test with a realistic expiration and avoid prematurely submitting the form. Apply appropriate data retention and privacy measures.
Detailed guidance

Authentication sessions protect accounts, but expiration can happen while a user is composing an answer or gathering information. Losing their work can disproportionately affect users who need longer to read, enter text or use assistive technology.

The requirement is to continue the activity without loss of data after re-authentication. This is more than returning to the same URL: answers, selected options and the current step may need to be restored. Preserve only the necessary information using storage and retention appropriate to the application, user expectations and privacy obligations.

In a test environment, expire the session after entering distinctive values, sign in again and verify that the user returns to the unfinished task. Check that the restoration does not submit or share the draft unexpectedly. Consider what happens if re-authentication fails or is canceled and communicate the next step.
Worked verification

Test the session-expiry path with realistic unfinished work rather than an empty form. Enter several values, allow the session to expire, reauthenticate, and compare the restored values and current step with the state before expiry. Confirm that restoration does not silently submit the application. Protect drafts on shared devices and decide how long they are retained; preserving data must not accidentally expose it to another person.
Further explanation and testing

Authentication expiry may be necessary, but losing work because of it can impose a disproportionate burden on someone who uses assistive technology or needs more time. The criterion addresses the ability to continue an activity without data loss after reauthentication. It applies to the state of the task, not just the ability to reach the sign-in page again.

A multi-step application can save an in-progress draft, request sign-in when the session ends, and return the person to the same step with prior answers intact. Do not automatically submit a partially completed form when the user signs in again. Choose storage and retention carefully: draft data may be sensitive, and returning it to a different person on a shared device would introduce a separate problem.

Create a realistic draft with entries on several steps, allow or simulate session expiry, then sign in again and compare the recovered data. Test validation messages, selected options, uploaded material where applicable, and the current step. Verify that the session is genuinely expired rather than merely showing a mock dialog, and check what happens if the user chooses not to sign in immediately.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Enter a name, choose an option, and type a long explanation in a multi-step application. Let the session expire, sign in as the same user, and compare all three values and the current step. A page that returns the user to the correct step but silently clears the explanation still loses data. Test the case where the user signs in later rather than immediately. The draft must be protected so another person using the same device cannot see it, and it should not be submitted automatically while the user is reauthenticating.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Save an unfinished application as a protected draft keyed to the authenticated user. When the session expires, prompt for authentication and restore the same draft and current task afterward. Test with several distinct values so partial loss is visible. Check files and multi-step selections when the product supports them; restoring the first field alone is not enough. Do not submit automatically after login. On a shared computer, verify that a different account cannot retrieve the draft, and apply the product’s retention policy consistently. A user may still need notice about inactivity-related loss under 2.2.6.
Worked example and edge cases

A user is halfway through a benefits application when the authentication session expires. After signing in again, the application should restore the user's work and allow the same activity to continue without data loss. Test text fields, selected options, uploaded attachments where applicable, and the current step. Also verify that re-authentication does not silently submit the application. Protect stored drafts according to the sensitivity of the data and the shared-device context; persistence must not expose the information to the next person who uses the device. Try both an expired session and a normal sign-out and document which behaviors belong to each scenario.
Planning a thorough review

When a feature depends on time, map the point at which a timer starts, the event that ends it, and the consequence for the user's task. Read the interface copy and then observe the actual server behavior; a visible countdown can differ from the expiration enforced on the server. Check what happens to entered information before expiry, at expiry, and after a return to the task. Use a test account and sample data so that losing a draft does not affect a real user. If an extension or preference is offered, check its actual effect and whether it remains understandable and operable with a keyboard.

Different timing criteria protect different outcomes. A warning about data loss is not necessarily a way to extend a time limit; a pause for moving content is not necessarily a way to resume an expired session. Apply the conditions and exceptions of the specific criterion in the lesson, rather than treating every timer as the same case. For any exception, describe the real function and why the conditions apply. Product convenience, advertising schedules, or a general preference for short sessions are not automatically proof that a time limit or interruption is essential.
Required practical activity
Enter a multi-step form, force a session expiry, log back in and verify the draft and current step are restored.
Knowledge check
What should happen after a session expires during a form?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.2.6 Timeouts
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.2.6 Timeouts (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.2.6 Timeouts (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Warn users about the period of inactivity that may cause loss of entered data, unless the data is preserved for more than 20 hours while the user takes no action.
Implementation and testing
Explain the actual inactivity duration before a user risks losing work. Saving a draft can reduce the risk, but its retention and privacy implications should be considered separately.
Real-world example: the barrier
An application silently deletes an unfinished draft after fifteen minutes of inactivity. A learner who pauses to consult notes returns to an empty form.
Improved design and verification
Inform the learner of the inactivity period that risks data loss, unless the actual preservation period meets the more-than-20-hours exception. Check that the warning matches system behavior.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A draft is deleted after inactivity without any warning.
Improved approach:
Tell the user the inactivity duration that can cause data loss before they risk it.
Verify that the actual retention period matches the message; an exception applies when data remains preserved for more than 20 hours of inactivity.
Detailed guidance

Users should know how long inactivity can cause data to be lost before relying on the application to keep a draft. A timeout may differ from session expiry: an account can remain signed in while an unsaved draft is removed, or a session can expire while a draft remains preserved.

State the relevant period in language that matches actual behavior. If inactivity of fifteen minutes discards entered answers, tell the user that before the loss occurs. The criterion provides an exception when the data is preserved for more than 20 hours of inactivity; exactly 20 hours does not meet that wording.

Test the server behavior, not only a countdown shown in the interface. Enter data, stop interacting for the documented period and verify what remains. Consider privacy and consent when retaining drafts, especially on shared devices; preserving data longer should be designed deliberately rather than assumed to be risk-free.
Worked verification

A useful warning identifies the period of inactivity and the consequence, for example: “Your unsaved answers will be deleted after 15 minutes of inactivity.” Place this information before users risk losing work, and verify it against the actual retention behavior. A warning that says only “session expires soon” does not explain that answers may be lost. Test both the stated duration and any longer-than-20-hours preservation exception.
Further explanation and testing

An inactivity timeout can destroy work even when a person has not left the task voluntarily: they may be reading instructions, using another device, or taking a break. This criterion requires notice of the duration of user inactivity that could cause data loss, unless the data is preserved for more than 20 hours when the user takes no action.

Make the warning specific enough to guide a choice before the loss occurs. “Your unsaved answers will be removed after 15 minutes of inactivity” identifies both duration and consequence. A generic message that a session may expire does not necessarily tell the person what will happen to their work. If the service retains the draft for more than 20 hours, verify the actual retention period rather than assuming that a background save lasts indefinitely.

Compare the warning with the server-side behavior using a safe test draft. Remain inactive for the stated interval, return, and inspect whether the data remains available. If the product changes its timeout or draft-retention policy, update the warning as well. Consider the related reauthentication and timing criteria independently: explaining a data-loss risk is not the same as enabling a user to extend a time limit.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A form warns “Your session may expire,” but the server removes unsaved answers after 15 minutes of inactivity. Revise the message to state that period and the potential loss of answers, and place it where the user can encounter it before relying on the form. Test with a safe draft and verify the server’s actual behavior. If the service instead preserves all entered data for more than 20 hours of inactivity, document and test that retention rather than relying on an assumption about browser storage.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A form that deletes unsaved entries after 15 minutes should disclose that duration and consequence before the person risks loss. Compare the displayed message with server behavior using a test draft and an actual inactivity interval. A message about automatic sign-out is incomplete if it does not explain that entered answers will be lost. If data is preserved for more than 20 hours while the user takes no action, verify that retention rather than assuming a browser cache persists. Keep the disclosure in sync when the timeout or data-retention policy changes.
Worked example and edge cases

Before a learner begins a long form, tell them how much inactivity can lead to losing entered work, unless the data is preserved for more than twenty hours of inactivity. The warning must reflect the actual behavior: a message promising an hour is misleading if the server removes the draft after fifteen minutes. Check when the inactivity period starts, what actions reset it, and whether a saved draft survives a network interruption. This criterion concerns warning about possible data loss; a separate timing requirement can apply to the time limit itself. Do not assume that satisfying one of these requirements automatically satisfies the other.
Planning a thorough review

When a feature depends on time, map the point at which a timer starts, the event that ends it, and the consequence for the user's task. Read the interface copy and then observe the actual server behavior; a visible countdown can differ from the expiration enforced on the server. Check what happens to entered information before expiry, at expiry, and after a return to the task. Use a test account and sample data so that losing a draft does not affect a real user. If an extension or preference is offered, check its actual effect and whether it remains understandable and operable with a keyboard.

Different timing criteria protect different outcomes. A warning about data loss is not necessarily a way to extend a time limit; a pause for moving content is not necessarily a way to resume an expired session. Apply the conditions and exceptions of the specific criterion in the lesson, rather than treating every timer as the same case. For any exception, describe the real function and why the conditions apply. Product convenience, advertising schedules, or a general preference for short sessions are not automatically proof that a time limit or interruption is essential.
Required practical activity
Write an inactivity warning for an unsaved form and verify it matches the application’s actual timeout behavior.
Knowledge check
When is a warning about inactivity-related data loss required under this criterion?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.
