lessons.title: 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Flashing content can trigger seizures. At Level A, content must not flash more than three times in any one second unless it is below both applicable general and red flash thresholds.
Implementation and testing

The thresholds depend on properties including the area and characteristics of the flash; visual inspection alone is not a reliable assessment. Prefer static feedback and use an appropriate flash analysis tool if flashing is unavoidable.
Real-world example: the barrier
A large red error banner flashes rapidly to draw attention. A person with photosensitive epilepsy may be exposed before they can choose to stop it.
Improved design and verification
Use a static error message and icon. If an effect must flash, evaluate the actual flash rate and both relevant threshold definitions using suitable tools.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A large red alert flashes rapidly.
Improved approach:
Show a static alert and explanatory text.
A pause button alone does not demonstrate conformance with flash thresholds. Evaluate the content itself with suitable analysis when necessary.
Detailed guidance

Flashing involves alternating changes in luminance that can trigger photosensitive seizures. Certain saturated red flashes receive particular attention in the threshold definitions. Large, rapid flashes can be hazardous even when the rest of a page is accessible.

The Level A rule permits no more than three flashes in any one-second period, unless the flashing falls below the specified general and red flash thresholds. Those thresholds are not a simple guess about whether a graphic looks small. Assess the actual rendered content, including video, animated advertisements and overlays, with an appropriate analysis method.

The safest ordinary design is to avoid rapid flashes: use stable text, a static icon or a non-flashing status change. A pause control does not by itself establish that hazardous content meets the flash requirement. The related AAA 2.3.2 removes the threshold alternative.
Worked verification

When evaluating a flashing video, examine the rendered content over time rather than checking only a still image. The general and red-flash thresholds depend on technical characteristics, including affected area, and both must be considered when relying on the threshold exception. A pause control does not prevent exposure before it is found. If the visual effect is unnecessary, removing the flash is a more straightforward design.
Further explanation and testing

Repeated flashes can trigger seizures for some people with photosensitive epilepsy. This risk concerns changes in luminance or saturated red over time, rather than ordinary motion alone. Because a person can be exposed as soon as content is displayed, an optional pause control is not a substitute for evaluating the flashing itself.

At Level A, content must not flash more than three times in any one-second period, or the flash must remain below both the general flash and red flash thresholds. The threshold evaluation depends on technical properties, including the area and characteristics of the flashing content. Use suitable analysis rather than assuming a small or brief animation is harmless from a casual glance.

Audit application animations, videos, advertising, and embedded material that the author controls. The simplest repair for a flashing error banner is often static text and an icon, which still communicate the problem without the effect. When flashing is retained, inspect the rendered sequence using a suitable tool and document the relevant interval and thresholds. The stricter AAA 2.3.2 criterion does not include the below-threshold alternative.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A red alert alternates with the background four times in one second. Do not assume that it is acceptable simply because it lasts only briefly or provides a Stop button. Replace it with a static alert where possible. If the effect is necessary, examine the rendered sequence with an appropriate flash analysis tool and evaluate both the general and red thresholds in the context of the criterion. Include embedded media the page author controls. Record the tested version and interval so a later animation change can be rechecked.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Replace a rapidly alternating red error banner with static text, an error icon, and a clear heading. The information remains available without requiring a visual flash to attract attention. If a flash is retained, analyze the rendered content over the relevant one-second interval and evaluate the applicable general and red flash thresholds with suitable tools. A small apparent area, a short clip, or an optional pause button alone does not establish compliance. Repeat analysis when an embedded video or animation is edited; a safe still image says nothing about the sequence of changes over time.
Worked example and edge cases

An alert animation alternates bright red and dark backgrounds four times in one second. Replace the effect with a static message and icon when the flash is not necessary. When an effect remains, evaluate the actual rendered sequence and the general and red flash thresholds with an appropriate analysis method; a still screenshot cannot establish the number or nature of flashes. Inspect embedded advertisements and video as well as first-party UI. The Level A rule allows content that does not exceed three flashes in any one-second period, or that remains below both applicable thresholds. A pause control alone does not demonstrate that the flashing content meets either condition.
Planning a thorough review

Review both the content and the conditions under which it appears. An animation may be harmless in its resting state but begin after a user opens a menu, receives an error, or changes a setting. Identify whether the issue is flashing, interaction-triggered motion, or both, then apply the corresponding criterion. A control to pause moving content addresses a different requirement and should not be assumed to establish that rapid flashes are safe. When flashing must be assessed against thresholds, use an appropriate analysis method for the rendered media; do not infer compliance from a single still image.

For motion-sensitive users, test preferences before triggering the effect and check that disabling motion leaves the underlying information and controls available. Examine first-party transitions and embedded material, including loading, success, and failure states. Document the exact state, viewport, sequence, and relevant preference used during testing so another reviewer can reproduce the observation. If a team believes an effect is essential, explain what information or function would be lost without it; visual polish alone does not establish that the animation is essential.
Required practical activity
Replace a rapidly flashing error animation with static text and an icon. Explain why judging safety from a short casual glance is insufficient.
Knowledge check
What is a safer alternative to a rapidly flashing error message?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.3.2 Three Flashes
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.3.2 Three Flashes (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.3.2 Three Flashes (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
The AAA criterion prohibits more than three flashes in any one-second period; unlike 2.3.1, it does not offer the below-threshold alternative.
Implementation and testing
Remove rapid flashes from animations, advertisements and embedded media. Count changes using the WCAG definition of a flash and test the actual rendered content.
Real-world example: the barrier
A small decorative badge flashes four times per second. Its designer assumes the small area automatically makes it acceptable at AAA.
Improved design and verification
Remove the rapid flashing. The AAA criterion does not retain the below-threshold exception available at Level A.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A four-flashes-per-second badge is assumed acceptable because it is small.
Improved approach:
Remove the rapid flashes regardless of their area for this AAA target.
The below-threshold exception available under 2.3.1 is not part of this enhanced criterion.
Detailed guidance

At AAA, a page must not contain anything that flashes more than three times in any one-second period. Unlike 2.3.1, this rule does not permit more frequent flashes merely because they fall below the general and red thresholds.

Review advertisements, video, progress effects and error treatments, not just the application’s own CSS. Replace rapid flashing with stable feedback wherever possible. A warning that appears before flashing does not remove the flashing from the page.

Analyze an actual representative second of rendered content using the WCAG definition of a flash and suitable tools. An animation can contain bright changes that are not automatically equivalent to flashes, so count based on the definition rather than guessing from the number of frames.
Worked verification

Compare this enhanced requirement with the Level A criterion before evaluating a small flashing icon. At Level A, a sequence may fall below the relevant thresholds even if it flashes more than three times per second. For this AAA criterion, that below-threshold alternative is not available. Review advertisements and embedded videos as well as application-owned animation, and inspect any one-second interval rather than averaging over a whole clip.
Further explanation and testing

This enhanced seizure criterion limits flashes to no more than three in any one-second period. It differs from Level A 2.3.1 because the latter also allows content that remains below both applicable flash thresholds. A small flashing region that meets the Level A threshold alternative can still exceed the rate permitted by this AAA criterion.

Averages across an entire video can hide a short rapid sequence. Examine the interval containing the fastest changes and apply the WCAG definition of a flash when counting. A low overall average does not make a burst of four flashes in a single second acceptable under the enhanced criterion.

Replace an attention-grabbing flash with static emphasis or a non-flashing state change when possible. Inspect authored animation, embedded video, and third-party promotional content in the actual page. If content changes dynamically, test the states users will encounter, not only the first frame. Check separately whether motion triggered by interaction can be disabled under 2.3.3.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A tiny badge flashes four times in one second and passes the applicable Level A threshold analysis. It can still fail this enhanced criterion because the below-threshold alternative is not present here. Slow or remove the flashing and inspect the most rapid one-second interval. A long video with only one short burst deserves the same examination of that burst; averaging flashes over the complete video could conceal the problem. Test the actual rendered animation rather than inferring its rate from a design mockup.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A four-flashes-per-second badge may qualify under a threshold alternative at Level A yet still fail this enhanced criterion, which does not include that alternative. Remove or slow the flash, then inspect the fastest one-second interval of the rendered sequence. Do not average the total flashes over a long video: a brief burst can exceed the allowed rate even when the overall average looks low. Review third-party content controlled by the page author as well as the site’s own animation. A user-controlled pause is not a replacement for evaluating the rate.
Worked example and edge cases

A small status badge flashes four times within one second. The designer argues that it occupies a tiny portion of the page, but the enhanced requirement does not retain the threshold alternative from the Level A criterion. Remove the rapid flashing and provide a persistent status label or other nonflashing feedback. Inspect the actual sequence over every one-second interval; an average across a longer animation can conceal a burst of rapid flashes. Review loading indicators, notifications, embedded content, and animations on error, including states that appear only after a network failure.
Planning a thorough review

Review both the content and the conditions under which it appears. An animation may be harmless in its resting state but begin after a user opens a menu, receives an error, or changes a setting. Identify whether the issue is flashing, interaction-triggered motion, or both, then apply the corresponding criterion. A control to pause moving content addresses a different requirement and should not be assumed to establish that rapid flashes are safe. When flashing must be assessed against thresholds, use an appropriate analysis method for the rendered media; do not infer compliance from a single still image.

For motion-sensitive users, test preferences before triggering the effect and check that disabling motion leaves the underlying information and controls available. Examine first-party transitions and embedded material, including loading, success, and failure states. Document the exact state, viewport, sequence, and relevant preference used during testing so another reviewer can reproduce the observation. If a team believes an effect is essential, explain what information or function would be lost without it; visual polish alone does not establish that the animation is essential.
Required practical activity
Compare a four-flash-per-second animation with a static notification and explain the AAA outcome.
Knowledge check
How does 2.3.2 differ from 2.3.1?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Motion animation triggered by interaction can cause dizziness or nausea. At AAA it must be possible to disable it unless essential to the functionality or information.
Implementation and testing
Respect reduced-motion preferences where possible and offer a setting when needed. Replace a zooming transition with an immediate state change while retaining the content and controls.
Real-world example: the barrier
A settings panel zooms across the entire viewport when opened. A user sensitive to motion becomes dizzy before reaching its controls.
Improved design and verification
Provide a reduced-motion setting that replaces the zoom with an immediate transition. Verify that the same settings remain available.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
.panel { transition: transform 700ms; }
Improved approach:
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .panel { transition: none; } }
Ensure the state change and information still work without motion. A site setting can provide additional control.
Detailed guidance

Motion triggered by interaction can produce dizziness or nausea for some users. Examples include a large panel flying across the screen after a button press, parallax movement during scrolling and animated zoom transitions. This AAA requirement concerns motion animation triggered by interaction, with an exception when it is essential to the function or information.

Allow the animation to be disabled while keeping the result available. Respecting the operating system’s reduced-motion preference is a useful technique; an application-specific preference can also give users control. Replacing motion with an immediate state change or a subtle non-motion cue preserves the action without requiring the same visual effect.

Test with the preference enabled and disabled, including menus, dialogs, scrolling and route changes. Verify that disabling animation does not remove the destination, feedback or control. Separately assess automatic movement under 2.2.2 and flashing under 2.3.1; one setting does not settle every motion-related criterion.
Worked verification

Test the preference before opening the interface, because a user should not have to experience the problematic animation in order to disable it. With reduced motion enabled, trigger the same menu, route change, and dialog as in the default mode. Verify that content appears in the correct place and that focus is still managed. A brief opacity change may be less disruptive than large movement, but user controls and the actual effect still need evaluation.
Further explanation and testing

Motion triggered by a user action can cause dizziness, nausea, or disorientation for people with vestibular sensitivities. Large zooms, parallax effects, and sliding whole panels can be especially problematic. The AAA criterion requires interaction-triggered motion animation to be disableable unless the animation is essential to the functionality or information.

Respecting the operating system reduced-motion preference is a useful implementation technique. For example, a CSS media query can remove a transform transition and show the final state immediately. A site-level setting can provide additional control. The destination content, interaction, and focus behavior must remain available when motion is reduced; disabling the animation should not disable the task.

Enable reduced motion before starting the page, then open menus, switch routes, and display dialogs. Compare the content and controls with the default mode and check for movement introduced by JavaScript or embedded components as well as CSS. If a motion is claimed to be essential, explain what information or functionality would be lost without it instead of treating a decorative transition as essential.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Opening a navigation drawer causes the whole viewport to slide and zoom. Enable the operating system reduced-motion preference before loading the page, then open the drawer. The destination and focus behavior should remain usable even if the transition is removed. Inspect scripts as well as CSS: a JavaScript animation can continue after a CSS transition has been disabled. Test any site-level motion preference separately and confirm that the user can reach it without first triggering a large animation.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A drawer that slides across the screen can use a reduced-motion media query to replace its transform transition with an immediate state change. Turn on the preference before opening the drawer, and verify that its controls and focus behavior remain available. Inspect JavaScript-driven animations too: disabling CSS transition does not stop a script that moves the element frame by frame. If a product offers a separate motion setting, ensure it is reachable without triggering the animation first. Record any claimed essential exception with a reason tied to the information or function.
Worked example and edge cases

Opening a drawer causes the whole page to zoom and slide. A person who experiences vestibular symptoms should be able to disable nonessential interaction-triggered motion. Test with the operating system's reduced-motion preference enabled before opening the page, and inspect any application-level setting as well. The drawer should still open, show the same controls, and put focus in an appropriate place without requiring the user to experience the unwanted transition first. Distinguish motion animation from a simple change of state, and document any claim that an animation is essential to functionality or information rather than merely attractive.
Planning a thorough review

Review both the content and the conditions under which it appears. An animation may be harmless in its resting state but begin after a user opens a menu, receives an error, or changes a setting. Identify whether the issue is flashing, interaction-triggered motion, or both, then apply the corresponding criterion. A control to pause moving content addresses a different requirement and should not be assumed to establish that rapid flashes are safe. When flashing must be assessed against thresholds, use an appropriate analysis method for the rendered media; do not infer compliance from a single still image.

For motion-sensitive users, test preferences before triggering the effect and check that disabling motion leaves the underlying information and controls available. Examine first-party transitions and embedded material, including loading, success, and failure states. Document the exact state, viewport, sequence, and relevant preference used during testing so another reviewer can reproduce the observation. If a team believes an effect is essential, explain what information or function would be lost without it; visual polish alone does not establish that the animation is essential.
Required practical activity
Enable reduced motion, activate a menu and compare the interaction with its animated version. Confirm the same information remains available.
Knowledge check
What is an appropriate alternative to a large animated zoom transition?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Repeated navigation and other blocks force keyboard users to traverse the same material on each page. A bypass mechanism lets users reach the unique content efficiently.
Implementation and testing
Place a visible-on-focus skip link early in the page and connect it to the main content. Semantic landmarks and other mechanisms can also help; test the actual focus movement and reading position.
Real-world example: the barrier
A site repeats forty navigation links before the main content on every page. A keyboard user must pass each link on every visit.
Improved design and verification
Add an early skip link that moves users to main content, and test its focus behavior after activation. Verify that the destination is not hidden under a sticky header.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A keyboard user must tab through every repeated menu on every page.
Improved approach:

Skip to main content ...
...
The ellipsis represents intervening page markup. Verify that activating the link moves reading position and that keyboard focus continues sensibly.
Detailed guidance

Repeated blocks such as site navigation, promotional links and account controls appear on many pages. A person navigating by keyboard or linear reading may otherwise traverse the same material repeatedly before reaching the content that changes.

A skip link near the beginning of the page can point to the main content. Its destination needs a valid unique identifier, and the link must be available to keyboard users. A link that remains invisible when focused or points to a nonexistent target is not a useful bypass. Semantic landmarks and other methods can also provide navigation mechanisms; test the method in the supported environment.

Load a page from the browser address bar, press Tab and activate the bypass. Verify that the user reaches the intended main region and can continue navigating from there. Repeat on pages with sticky headers and different layouts, because the destination may otherwise be obscured or the subsequent focus order may return to the navigation.
Worked verification

Start at the browser address bar, move focus into the page, and look for the bypass control before navigating through repeated links. Activate it and check both the visible destination and the next Tab stop. A link that scrolls to the main region but leaves sequential focus among the navigation links may not provide the expected keyboard experience. Repeat on a second page with the same navigation and with a sticky header present.
Further explanation and testing

Repeated blocks can include a site-wide navigation menu, search area, or other content appearing before the main part of many pages. A keyboard user who must move through every repeated link on each visit spends time before reaching the task. A bypass mechanism provides a shorter route; the requirement concerns repeated blocks rather than demanding a particular visual design for every page.

A common implementation places a skip link near the start of the document and links it to the main region. Make it visible when focused so a keyboard user can discover it, and ensure the target exists. A target may need to receive programmatic focus to give a reliable keyboard experience in the supported environment. Landmarks or other mechanisms can also help, depending on how users access the page.

Starting at the browser chrome, Tab into the page and activate the bypass mechanism. Check where the page scrolls, where focus lands, and what happens on the next Tab. A sticky header must not obscure the destination. Repeat on representative pages with shared navigation and after client-side route changes. A link that only looks like a skip control but has a broken fragment target does not provide the intended route.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Add a “Skip to main content” link as the first page control and point it to the main region. Start from the browser address bar, Tab into the page, activate the link, and press Tab again. Verify that the next control is in the main task rather than back in the repeated menu. Check that the target is not obscured by a fixed header. Repeat after navigating to another route, because a fragment target that exists on one page may be missing from another.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Put Skip to main content near the beginning of the page and provide a main region with the matching id. If the target needs programmatic focus for the supported browsers, implement and test that behavior. Starting from browser chrome, Tab to the link, activate it, and press Tab again. The user should reach the main task without traversing the repeated navigation. A fixed header should not cover the target. Repeat on each route: a correct link with a missing or duplicate target on one page does not provide a reliable bypass there.
Worked example and edge cases

On every page of a documentation site, forty navigation links precede the main article. Put a skip link early in the focus order so that a keyboard user can bypass the repeated block. Starting from the browser chrome, Tab into the page, activate the link, and then press Tab again. Check that the destination is visible, the next focus stop belongs to the main content, and a fixed header has not covered the destination. Repeat after navigating to another page. A landmark or other mechanism may also be appropriate, but simply adding an invisible link without verifying its destination and focus behavior is not a useful bypass.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Tab from the browser into a page, activate its skip link and confirm that subsequent keyboard navigation starts at the main content.
Knowledge check
What should a skip link help a user do?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.2 Page Titled
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
A page title identifies the topic or purpose in browser tabs, history and assistive technology. Generic or repeated titles make pages difficult to distinguish.
Implementation and testing
Set a descriptive document title such as “Payment details – Store”. Update it after client-side route changes and include meaningful context when an error state changes the page.
Real-world example: the barrier
Five different application screens all show “Home” in their browser tabs. A user cannot identify the desired screen from the tab list.
Improved design and verification
Give each document a title that describes its purpose and update it on route changes. Compare the tabs without looking at their page bodies.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
<title>Home</title> appears on every route.
Improved approach:
<title>Payment details – Example Store</title>
Update document.title when client-side navigation changes the page. The title should identify the actual page or task.
Detailed guidance

A document title appears in browser tabs, history, bookmarks and assistive technology. It gives a user an early way to distinguish the current page from other open pages. A visible heading alone does not replace a descriptive browser title.

Choose a concise title that identifies the page topic or purpose, usually followed by the site or application name. For multi-step flows, distinguish steps such as shipping and payment. For single-page applications, update the document title when navigation changes the page content; the browser tab should not remain stuck on the initial route.

Open several routes in separate tabs and read only their titles. Confirm that each is recognizable and that title changes follow navigation. If a form returns an error page, a title that identifies the error state may help users notice the change, while preserving the underlying page context.
Worked verification

Compare pages by using only their browser tabs or history entries. A title such as “Account” repeated for profile, security, and billing pages does not distinguish those tasks. Use titles that describe the current page and keep the site name as supporting context. In a single-page application, navigate without reloading and verify that the document title changes when the route changes, including when using the browser Back button.
Further explanation and testing

The document title appears in browser tabs, history, bookmarks, and assistive technology announcements. It provides context before someone examines the body of the page. Titles that are blank or repeatedly say “Home” make it hard to distinguish a payment form from an account page when several tabs are open.

Describe the actual topic or purpose first, followed by supporting site context when useful: “Payment details – Example Store” is more informative than “Example Store.” In a single-page application, the browser may keep the same document loaded while the visible route changes, so update document.title as part of navigation. A title should reflect the current state, not just the name of the application shell.

Open several representative pages in separate tabs and identify each using only its title. Navigate between routes using links and the browser Back button and verify that the title tracks the visible page. Review dynamically generated titles for missing data and duplicated separators. A meaningful heading inside the page remains useful, but it does not replace a descriptive document title.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Open Account, Security, and Billing pages in separate tabs. If all three tabs are called “Dashboard,” rewrite their document titles so the page purpose is distinguishable. Navigate between those screens through client-side links and then use Back and Forward; the title should continue to match the displayed route. Test an error or loading state as well, because route metadata may be missing or stale. A heading in the page body is useful, but a person choosing among browser tabs cannot rely on it.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Set an initial title such as “Payment details – Example Store” and update document.title after client-side navigation. Open payment, shipping, and account screens in separate tabs and identify them from the tab labels. Then navigate with Back and Forward and verify the title changes with the displayed route. A route that fails to update the title can leave a user believing they are still on the previous screen. Check error and loading routes for missing title data. The visible heading is also useful, but a browser-tab user needs the document title.
Worked example and edge cases

A browser tab labeled “Home” provides little help when it actually contains the payment step of a checkout. Change the document title to identify the current purpose, such as “Payment details — Example Store.” Open several pages in separate tabs and compare only their titles to see whether a user can distinguish them. In a single-page application, navigate through the router and use browser Back and Forward; the document title should track the current view rather than remaining on the first route. Include useful state information when it helps identify the current page, but avoid making the title so long that its distinguishing words are hidden.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Open three application pages in tabs and compare their titles. Rewrite ambiguous titles so each page can be identified without inspecting its body.
Knowledge check
Which browser title best identifies a checkout step?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.3 Focus Order
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Sequential focus must preserve meaning and operability when order affects understanding or interaction. Visual layout, DOM order and script-driven focus can diverge.
Implementation and testing

Use a logical DOM order and avoid positive tabindex values as a shortcut. When opening a dialog, move focus into it and restore focus sensibly when it closes. Check responsive layouts and dynamically inserted errors.
Real-world example: the barrier
A purchase dialog visually presents shipping, billing and payment in order, but keyboard focus jumps from shipping to the footer and back into payment.
Improved design and verification
Correct the source or focus-management order so users encounter controls in an understandable sequence. Check the sequence after the dialog opens and when it closes.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
Positive tabindex values force focus to jump between unrelated fields.
Improved approach:
Arrange controls in a meaningful DOM order and use ordinary sequential focus.
Test visual order, DOM order and script-driven focus at multiple viewport sizes; sequential order must preserve meaning and operation.
Detailed guidance

Focus order is the sequence in which a person reaches interactive elements using sequential keyboard navigation. It is often based on document order, but positive tabindex values, script-managed focus and visual layout techniques can produce a different sequence. A jump is a problem when it changes the meaning or prevents the user from operating the interface; a single universal left-to-right order is not required in every design.

Consider a form that visually displays a label and field for name, then email, then a submit button. If keyboard focus moves from name to submit before email, the form can appear to be complete before a required field has been encountered. Similarly, when an error summary appears after submission, users need a coherent route from the summary to each invalid field and back to completion.

Prefer meaningful source order and ordinary controls. Avoid using positive tabindex values to repair a broken layout because those values are difficult to maintain as components are added or removed. For dialogs, deliberately place focus where the user can understand the new context; when closing, restore it to the opener or another logical location. Do not move focus merely because a visual animation has occurred.

Test at normal and increased zoom and after switching to a narrow viewport. CSS layout can change while source order remains the same. Write down the sequence in which controls receive focus, including dynamically revealed controls. Confirm that focus does not jump behind an open modal and that closing it permits the task to continue.
Further explanation and testing

Sequential focus order is the path followed by Tab and Shift+Tab. It matters when the sequence affects meaning or operation: a person should encounter a control in a context that makes sense and be able to complete a task without unexpected jumps. The sequence need not match visual placement in every situation, but discrepancies that change the meaning or break the workflow must be corrected.

Start with document order. CSS can visually rearrange items without changing their position in the DOM, and positive tabindex values can create a separate sequence that is difficult to maintain. Rather than assigning arbitrary positive numbers, arrange the source in a meaningful order and use normal focus behavior. Check layouts at narrow widths, where columns may stack in a different order, and check dynamically inserted controls such as validation messages.

When a dialog opens, send focus to an appropriate element inside it so the user knows the context has changed. While the dialog is active, manage its focus according to its interaction pattern, and provide a usable way to close it. After closing, restore focus to a logical location, usually the opener. Test forward and backward movement before, inside, and after the dialog; inspect the behavior when the opener has been removed or the form has reported errors.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A checkout visually shows shipping, billing, and payment, but CSS places the payment panel first in DOM order. Tab through the task at desktop and narrow widths, writing down each control encountered. Reorder the markup or layout so the sequence preserves meaning. For a dialog opened from the checkout, test focus as it enters, moves within, and leaves the dialog. An arbitrary sequence of positive tabindex values may appear to fix one viewport but can break again when controls are added.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Keep fields in a meaningful DOM order and use layout CSS without creating an unrelated keyboard sequence. Tab through the form while recording the order, then reverse with Shift+Tab. Repeat after a narrow viewport stacks columns and after validation inserts an error. When a dialog opens, move focus to an appropriate location inside and return it logically on close. A jump to a footer between related form fields can disrupt the task even if every control is individually reachable. Avoid positive tabindex as a fragile patch for an underlying source-order problem.
Worked example and edge cases

A form is displayed as name, address, and payment, but positive tabindex values make focus jump from payment to the page footer and back to name. Fix the underlying source order or focus management rather than adding more positive tabindex values. Trace the sequence with Tab and Shift+Tab at desktop width, narrow width, and high zoom, because a layout can rearrange visually without changing document order. When a dialog opens, moves focus, and closes, inspect the surrounding sequence as well. The criterion allows more than one logical order, but the chosen order must preserve meaning and operation.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Tab through a form and a dialog at desktop and mobile widths. Draw the focus sequence and correct any jumps that make the task confusing.
Knowledge check
A form visually displays name then email, but focus jumps from email to an unrelated footer. What should be reviewed?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context)
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

Users need to understand where a link leads from its text or its programmatically determined context, subject to the general-ambiguity exception. Context must be available to assistive technology, not merely placed visually nearby.
Implementation and testing
Prefer descriptive text such as “Read the refund policy”. If the same short label appears in a structured list or table, test that its relevant context is actually associated and announced.
Real-world example: the barrier
A list of articles contains repeated “Read more” links without an accessible relationship to each article heading. A screen reader user cannot identify the destination.
Improved design and verification
Use a distinctive link name or programmatically available context, such as a meaningful structured association. Test what is announced rather than relying on visual proximity.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
Click here without useful programmatic context.
Improved approach:
Read the refund policy
Distinct link text avoids relying on surrounding context; if context is used, ensure assistive technologies can determine it programmatically.
Detailed guidance

A link’s purpose should be clear from its text alone or from text together with its programmatically determined context, except where the purpose would be ambiguous to users generally. Visual proximity is not necessarily programmatic context: assistive technology needs the relationship to be represented by the document structure.

Descriptive link text is often the simplest solution. A link labeled “Read the refund policy” conveys more than “Click here”. In a list or table, surrounding structured context can sometimes establish the purpose, but repeated generic links still place extra demands on people who use a links list or navigate quickly.

Inspect links in context and through assistive technology. Check that identical names do not unexpectedly lead to different destinations without adequate context, and that the accessible name reflects what the link does. The AAA criterion 2.4.9 sets a stronger target for link text alone.
Worked verification

A link’s purpose may be determined from its text together with programmatically determined context under the stated conditions. Visually placing an article heading beside “Read more” does not automatically establish that association. Inspect the structure with a screen reader and compare how the link is announced in context. If context is unreliable or ambiguous, use a more specific label such as “Read the course registration guide.”
Further explanation and testing

Link purpose tells a person where a link goes or what it will do. Some users read links in a list, while others encounter each link within its paragraph or table. The Level A criterion permits the purpose to be determined from the link text alone or from link text together with programmatically determined context, except when the purpose would be ambiguous to users in general.

Use direct wording such as “Read the refund policy” when possible. Repeated “Read more” links may be understandable visually because headings appear nearby, but proximity alone does not prove that assistive technology can determine the association. If relying on context, inspect the actual structure and announcement in the relevant reading mode. Avoid misleading labels where different destinations use indistinguishable names.

Review a list of articles and record the text or accessible name of every link and its destination. Ask whether the purpose is clear in the relevant programmatic context. Test a screen reader as well as visual presentation, and check links that open files or external resources. The enhanced 2.4.9 criterion is stricter about link purpose from link text alone, so do not conflate the two levels.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A page lists three articles, each followed by a link labeled “Read more.” Inspect how a screen reader determines each link’s context and verify the destinations. If the relationship to the heading is not programmatically available, give each link an informative name such as “Read the enrollment guide.” The Level A criterion may allow programmatically determined context, but purely visual proximity is not proof of that relationship. Also verify that link wording does not promise a different destination from the one actually opened.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Replace an isolated Click here with a link whose text identifies the destination, such as “Read the refund policy.” If a design retains shorter link labels, test whether the permitted programmatic context is actually available to assistive technology. Merely placing a heading visually near a link is not proof of association. Compare the announced purpose with the destination and check repeated labels that point to different pages. At this level context can be permitted; the enhanced link-purpose criterion asks for purpose from link text alone subject to its exception.
Worked example and edge cases

A news page has three links called “Read more,” each beside a different story. Nearby text is not automatically programmatically determined context merely because it is visually close. Inspect each link in context with a screen reader and review the surrounding structure. If the applicable context does not make the destination clear, revise the link text to identify the story, for example “Read the housing policy update.” Compare this Level A requirement with the enhanced link-purpose criterion, which examines the link text itself. Repeated names are especially confusing when links lead to different destinations.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Inspect a list of “Read more” links. Rewrite them or verify their programmatic context identifies each destination.
Knowledge check
Which link communicates its purpose most reliably?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.5 Multiple Ways
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.5 Multiple Ways (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.5 Multiple Ways (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
People find pages in different ways. For a set of web pages, provide more than one way to locate each page, except pages that are results of or steps in a process.
Implementation and testing
Combine a consistent navigation system with search, a site map, or contextual links. Confirm that both methods really reach the intended page and are usable with keyboard and assistive technology.
Real-world example: the barrier
A support article can only be reached through one deep navigation menu, and the site search never indexes it. Users who do not know the menu hierarchy may not find it.
Improved design and verification
Make the article reachable through another working route, such as search or a site map. Confirm the article is not merely a step or result of a process before applying the exception.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
An article is reachable only through one deep menu.
Improved approach:
Offer both a navigation route and a working site search or site map.
Verify both routes actually lead to the article. A process step or result is covered by a specific exception.
Detailed guidance

Users search for information in different ways: some follow menus, others use search or a site map, and some arrive through contextual links. Providing more than one way to locate pages reduces dependence on remembering a single hierarchy.

The criterion applies to locating a web page within a set of web pages, with an exception for a page that is a step in or the result of a process. For example, a final confirmation screen may be tied to completing a transaction; that differs from a publicly available help article.

Pick several representative pages and trace two distinct working routes. Search must return the intended content, not merely be present as a decorative field. Test the routes with keyboard and verify that permissions or broken links do not make one route unusable.
Worked verification

Create an inventory of representative pages and record the routes users can take to reach each one. Search is a second method only if its index includes the page and its result actually opens it. Test navigation with the keyboard as well. A checkout confirmation or another page that is a step or result of a process has a specified exception; do not treat a normal help article as a process step simply because it links from a form.
Further explanation and testing

People may search for a page directly, browse categories, follow a site map, or use contextual links. A single navigation path assumes they understand the site’s structure in the same way as its authors. This criterion requires more than one way to locate a page within a set of web pages, except when the page is a step in or result of a process.

A documentation site might make a help article reachable through both a topic menu and search. A site map or a meaningful set of related links may serve a similar purpose. The methods must actually locate the intended page: a search field that excludes the article from its index is not a working second route. The process exception should be evaluated for the specific page, not applied to an entire application merely because it contains forms.

Choose representative pages across sections and follow at least two routes to each. Test search with realistic terms and verify the result opens the correct destination. Use keyboard navigation for each route and check that permission settings do not unexpectedly hide one route from the intended audience. Record pages with only one practical route and decide whether the process exception genuinely applies.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A help article is reachable from a menu but not returned by site search. Confirm the search index includes the article, search for a likely topic, and open the result with a keyboard. A menu and a search box are only two useful routes if both can reach the intended page. Record the routes for a sample of pages in each documentation section. A page that is a step in or result of a process may have an exception, but an ordinary help page linked from that process is not automatically such a step.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Make a documentation article reachable from a topic menu and from site search. Search for its topic using realistic words, open the result, and confirm it is the same page. An empty search index does not create a second route just because a search field is visible. A site map or meaningful contextual navigation can provide another path depending on the site. Sample pages across sections and note any with only one route. Evaluate the process-step exception for the specific page rather than assuming every page in an application qualifies.
Worked example and edge cases

An employee guide can be reached through a deep menu, but the site search does not index it and there is no site map entry. Add another working way to locate the guide, such as an indexed search result or a meaningful site map. Verify that the second method actually reaches the same page and is usable with a keyboard, rather than merely existing in the interface. The criterion has an exception for a page that is a step in, or result of, a process. A routine help article does not become a process result simply because it is linked from an application form.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Choose a help article and reach it through navigation and through search. Record any pages that have only one route.
Knowledge check
Which combination can provide multiple ways to locate a help page?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.6 Headings and Labels
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Headings and labels should describe the topic or purpose of the section or control they identify. Accurate labels help users scan, navigate and avoid mistakes.
Implementation and testing
Use specific headings and associate form labels with their inputs. A heading saying “Billing address” communicates more than “Details”; a label should identify what belongs in the field.
Real-world example: the barrier
A form has three controls all labeled “Details”, and a long article has headings named “More”. The labels and headings do not explain their purposes.
Improved design and verification
Replace them with precise names such as “Delivery address” and “Refund eligibility”. Associate each field label with its control and verify the heading structure.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
<label for="email">Details</label>
Improved approach:
<label for="email">Email address</label>
A descriptive label helps users understand the input, and the for/id relationship associates it with the field.
Detailed guidance

Headings and labels describe the purpose of sections and fields. A heading such as “Details” may be too broad when several sections contain different kinds of details; a label such as “Input” does not tell the user what information to enter.

Write labels that identify the expected information, such as “Delivery address” or “Email address”. Associate each label programmatically with its field so that clicking the label and using assistive technology identify the same control. Use headings that describe the following section rather than relying on size or color alone.

Review the interface without relying on surrounding visual cues. Ask whether each heading accurately describes its section and whether each field label distinguishes it from similar fields. This criterion addresses the descriptive quality of headings and labels; other criteria cover their programmatic relationships and instructions.
Worked verification

Ask a reviewer to scan the headings and field labels without reading the surrounding paragraphs. If several unrelated sections are called “Details,” the page gives little help in choosing a destination. Replace vague wording with labels tied to the actual task, then inspect the programmatic association between each label and input. A placeholder alone can disappear during entry and should not be relied on as a persistent label.
Further explanation and testing

A heading describes the topic of a section, while a label identifies the purpose of an input or other control. Both help people decide what to read or enter. Vague labels such as “Information” repeated across different form fields increase the chance of mistakes and make assistive technology navigation less useful.

Choose wording that describes the actual task: “Delivery address” distinguishes that field from “Billing address,” and “Refund eligibility” is more informative than “Details.” Associate labels with their form controls using the appropriate HTML relationship. A visible placeholder is not a durable replacement for a label because it can disappear once the user enters a value and may not provide the required association.

Review headings in isolation as a page outline and inspect form fields with their accessible names. Compare each heading with the section that follows and each label with the expected input. Test with both visual inspection and a screen reader or accessibility tree. A programmatically associated label can still be inadequate if its wording fails to describe the field’s purpose.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A form has three fields labeled “Address” for home, mailing, and billing details. Rename the labels to express each field’s purpose, then inspect the accessible name of every input. Next review a heading list where several sections are called “More information”; replace those headings with their actual topics. The label can be correctly associated and still be misleading, so evaluate its wording as well as the HTML association. Check the resulting labels after translation and when the form dynamically adds fields.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Give an email input a persistent label such as <label for="email">Email address</label> and connect it to the matching input id. Inspect the computed name and check that it describes what the user should enter. A correctly associated label reading “Details” can still be too vague. Review headings in the same way: “Payment method” is more useful than a repeated “More.” Test dynamically added fields and localized versions for broken associations or misleading duplicate labels. Placeholder text that disappears on entry should not serve as the sole persistent label.
Worked example and edge cases

A registration form uses “Details” for three unrelated field groups and “More” as the heading for several sections. Rewrite the labels to reflect their topics, such as “Delivery address” and “Payment method,” and connect each label to the appropriate control. Ask a reviewer to scan the headings and labels without reading all surrounding copy: they should be able to predict the subject or purpose. Inspect the accessibility tree to confirm that the name presented to assistive technology matches the intended label. A label can exist programmatically and still be too vague to describe the control's purpose.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Review a form with three fields labeled “Information”. Give each a specific label and check the accessible association.
Knowledge check
Which label best describes an email field?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.7 Focus Visible
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Keyboard users need a visible indication of which control has focus. Without it, the next key press may activate an unknown control.
Implementation and testing
Avoid removing browser outlines without a clear replacement. Test :focus-visible across links, buttons and custom widgets against their backgrounds and in high-contrast modes.
Real-world example: the barrier
A stylesheet removes outlines from links and buttons and supplies only a mouse-hover color. A keyboard user cannot see which item will activate.
Improved design and verification
Provide a visible keyboard focus style and test it across backgrounds and browser modes. Hover styling alone does not indicate keyboard focus.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
button:focus { outline: none; }
Improved approach:
button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #003eaa; outline-offset: 2px; }
Check visibility against the actual surrounding colors and in high-contrast environments; do not assume the color works everywhere.
Detailed guidance

Focus identifies which interface component receives keyboard input. A visible focus indicator lets someone predict whether Enter will open a link, submit a form or activate a button. Hover and selection are different states: a pointer may hover over one element while keyboard focus is on another, and a selected item need not be the currently focused item.

Browsers usually provide a default outline. Removing it globally with outline: none can erase the only position cue. If replacing a default style, provide a clear indicator for links, buttons, form inputs and custom widgets. The :focus-visible selector is useful for keyboard-oriented styling, but it should be tested in the browsers and modes the product supports.

A ring can disappear when its color blends into an adjacent background or when a parent clips it with overflow: hidden. Focus styles should be tested on light and dark surfaces, over images, when controls are disabled where applicable, and at high zoom. Forced-colors modes may transform author colors, so test whether the indicator remains apparent there as well.

Tab through a complete workflow and do not use the mouse to discover where you are. Record every control whose focus is ambiguous. WCAG 2.4.7 concerns the visibility of keyboard focus; the separate AAA Focus Appearance criterion has its own quantitative requirements. A style is not proven conformant simply because it uses an outline.
Further explanation and testing

The focus indicator tells a keyboard user which control will receive the next command. It is different from the mouse hover state and from the selected state of a tab or menu item. An interface can have a selected navigation item while focus is on another link, so both states must remain understandable. Removing the browser outline without a suitable replacement makes users guess where they are.

Use a visible style for keyboard focus on links, buttons, form fields, and custom controls. The :focus-visible selector can help distinguish keyboard-style focus from pointer interactions, but verify behavior in the browsers and components the product supports. A border that resembles the normal border, appears only on hover, or is covered by a neighboring element is not a useful indicator. Consider forced-colors and high-contrast settings as well as ordinary themes.

Walk through an entire task with Tab and Shift+Tab, watching the focused control at every step. Check on light and dark backgrounds, inside dialogs, and when the page is zoomed. Ask whether the indicator moves with focus and remains visible over both the component and surrounding surface. This criterion requires a visible mode of operation; the distinct AAA focus appearance criterion specifies additional measurements and exceptions.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A stylesheet sets outline: none on every button and uses a hover color to show interaction. Tab through the interface without moving the mouse: if no control visibly changes, the hover color does not solve the keyboard problem. Add a distinct focus-visible style and check it against both light and dark surfaces. Inspect custom widgets and links as well as buttons. Retest in forced-colors mode and at zoom, where borders or outlines may be clipped by a container.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Replace a global outline: none rule with a visible keyboard focus style, for example a sufficiently distinct outline on :focus-visible. Tab through links, buttons, form fields, and custom widgets on light and dark surfaces. A hover-only color does not reveal keyboard focus, and a selected menu item is not necessarily the focused item. Check that the ring is not clipped by overflow or covered by an adjacent component. Inspect the result in forced-colors mode and at zoom. The enhanced appearance criterion adds separate measurement requirements.
Worked example and edge cases

A custom stylesheet removes outlines from every control and relies on hover color alone. Someone navigating by keyboard cannot tell which button will activate. Add a visible focus indicator and test it against every background where the control appears, including dark mode, validation errors, and high-contrast settings. Tab through links, fields, menu items, and dialog controls; watch for clipping by overflow containers and for indicators hidden beneath sticky elements. Focus-visible styling can avoid unnecessary pointer focus decoration, but keyboard focus must remain visibly indicated. The enhanced focus appearance criterion adds separate measurable requirements and should not be conflated with this baseline criterion.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Tab through a navigation bar and form. Identify controls with no visible indicator, then apply and retest a distinct outline.
Knowledge check
What is an appropriate replacement for outline: none?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.
