lessons.title: 2.4.8 Location
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.8 Location (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.8 Location (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
At AAA, users can determine their location within a set of pages. Location cues help people understand their place in a larger site and return to nearby sections.
Implementation and testing
Use breadcrumbs, a current navigation item, or another clear indication as appropriate. Ensure the current state is communicated programmatically when applicable, for example with aria-current.
Real-world example: the barrier
A learner opens a documentation page from search and has no indication which topic and subtopic contain it.
Improved design and verification
Add a breadcrumb or current navigation indication that communicates location in the page set. Use appropriate semantics for the current page and test it with assistive technology.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
Every page uses an identical menu with no current-page indication.
Improved approach:
Docs / Keyboard
A breadcrumb should reflect the actual hierarchy; make sure the current location is identifiable to both visual and assistive-technology users.
Detailed guidance
At AAA, users have information about their location within a set of web pages. Someone arriving through a search engine may not know which section contains the page or how to reach related material.

A breadcrumb, current item in a consistent navigation system, or another location cue can provide this information. A breadcrumb should reflect a meaningful site hierarchy and identify the current location. When appropriate, use aria-current to communicate the current page programmatically.

Navigate directly to a deep page and check whether the location cue is understandable without first visiting its parent. Then follow the parent link and confirm the indication updates. Do not confuse the current focus indicator with the current page indication: one identifies keyboard position, the other location in the site.
Worked verification

A breadcrumb can show a path such as “Documentation > Forms > Error messages,” with the final item identifying the current page. Check that its hierarchy corresponds to the actual site structure and that earlier items navigate to meaningful parent pages. A current item in navigation is another possible location cue. Location within the site is different from the browser title: users need a way to understand where the current page sits among related pages.
Further explanation and testing

A page may be understandable on its own while still leaving a user uncertain where it sits in a larger site. Someone arriving from a search result may not know which documentation topic contains the current article or how to return to its parent section. This enhanced criterion requires information about the user’s location within a set of web pages.

A breadcrumb can show the path from a broader category to the current page. A navigation menu that clearly indicates the current item can also communicate location, depending on the structure. Use the actual hierarchy, not an invented sequence based only on the path the last user happened to take. Where appropriate, expose the current page programmatically, for example with aria-current.

Open an interior page directly, as if following a search result, and determine whether the location cue identifies both the current page and its relationship to the wider site. Test the parent links and the current-item announcement with keyboard and assistive technology. A descriptive browser title and a page heading help identify the page but do not necessarily explain its position in the site hierarchy.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Open a documentation article directly from a search result. A breadcrumb showing “Guides > Forms > Error messages” can explain its location without requiring the user to visit the parent pages first. Check that the parent items navigate to the corresponding sections and that the current item is correctly identified. A menu highlight can be another cue, but it must be visible and understandable when the page opens directly. Avoid showing a misleading breadcrumb based on a route that is not part of the site hierarchy.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A breadcrumb such as “Guides > Forms > Error messages” can identify the current article’s position in the documentation set. Use actual parent links and mark the current page programmatically when appropriate, for example with aria-current="page". Open the article directly from search and check that the cue still makes sense. Test the links with keyboard and a screen reader. A route title can identify the current page while failing to communicate where it sits among related pages, so inspect the hierarchy cue separately.
Worked example and edge cases

A learner lands directly on an article from search and cannot tell whether it belongs to forms, navigation, or media guidance. A breadcrumb such as “Guides > Forms > Error messages” can communicate the location within the larger set. Check that the earlier items lead to the expected parent pages and that the current page is correctly identified. A current item in a navigation menu can be another location cue. Inspect the location indicator on deep links and after client-side navigation; a breadcrumb that remains on the previous route can be worse than one that is absent. Distinguish the page's title from its location among related pages.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.

lessons.title: 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only)
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only) (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only) (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

At AAA, a mechanism allows link purpose to be identified from link text alone, except when purpose would be ambiguous to users generally. This supports users who navigate a list of links out of context.
Implementation and testing
Write self-contained link names such as “Download the annual report” instead of relying on a neighboring heading to explain “Download”. Check repeated links and accessible names.
Real-world example: the barrier
A screen reader links list contains ten links named “Read more”. Nearby article headings are not included in the list.
Improved design and verification
Give each link a self-contained name such as “Read the accessibility policy”. Confirm that the accessible link name still clearly identifies the destination.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
Read more
Improved approach:
Read the privacy policy
Inspect a standalone links list: the accessible link text should reveal its purpose without needing the surrounding paragraph.
Detailed guidance

Some screen reader users navigate a list of links detached from the surrounding paragraphs. Repeated “More” links can become indistinguishable even if a visual reader can infer their destinations from nearby headings.

The AAA criterion requires a mechanism to identify purpose from link text alone, except where that purpose would be ambiguous to users generally. Write self-contained names such as “Read the admission requirements” or “Download the 2025 report”. Ensure the accessible name and the visible wording work together.

Generate or inspect a links list and ask what each entry does without reading its paragraph. Check duplicate names that lead to different resources and verify file format or destination details where they are relevant to user choice. The related A criterion 2.4.4 permits programmatically determined context.
Worked verification

At the enhanced level, test the link text itself without relying on surrounding programmatically determined context. Open a screen reader links list and compare repeated names: ten links called “Read more” provide no distinction even when each is next to a different heading in the page. Revise each accessible link name to identify its destination, while keeping any visible label and accessible name compatible for speech input.
Further explanation and testing

The enhanced link-purpose criterion asks that the purpose of each link be identifiable from link text alone, except where its purpose would be ambiguous to users in general. This differs from the Level A criterion, which can permit programmatically determined context. The distinction is useful when a screen reader user reviews a list of links outside their surrounding paragraphs.

A list containing multiple “Read more” links forces the user to return to the surrounding content to determine which article each link opens. Replace them with names such as “Read the registration guide” and “Read the cancellation policy.” If adding visually hidden text or an accessible name, ensure that the visible label is still included in the accessible name where required for speech input.

Generate a links list, read each entry without its paragraph, and compare it with the destination. Check whether duplicate names lead to different places and whether the names meaningfully distinguish them. Review dynamic lists after data changes and after translation. Avoid adding long, repetitive prefixes that make scanning harder while trying to add context.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Open a screen reader links list for a page containing several “Download” links. If each downloads a different report, change the link names to identify the reports, such as “Download the 2025 accessibility report.” Verify that the visible label and accessible name remain compatible for voice users. Unlike the Level A link-purpose criterion, this enhanced criterion calls for purpose to be available from link text alone, subject to the general-ambiguity exception; surrounding table cells should not be assumed to solve every repeated link name.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A links list containing “Download,” “Download,” and “Download” does not distinguish three reports. Give the links names such as “Download the accessibility audit” and “Download the remediation plan.” Review those names without their surrounding paragraphs and compare each destination. If additional accessible text is used, keep the visible label in the computed name so speech users can invoke it. At this enhanced level, surrounding programmatically determined context should not be treated as a substitute for link text that identifies the purpose, subject to the criterion’s general-ambiguity exception.
Worked example and edge cases

A screen reader's links list shows ten entries named “Read more,” with no surrounding article headings. For this enhanced criterion, make each link's own text identify its purpose, for example “Read the accessible forms guide.” Review links in isolation, including icon-only controls whose accessible text may be generated by an accessible name. Avoid relying only on the paragraph or table cell that surrounds the link. When multiple links have the same purpose, consistent names can be appropriate; the important distinction is whether the link text identifies where or what the link leads to.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Extract all links from a page into a list and rewrite any labels whose destinations are unclear in isolation.
Knowledge check
Which link text can be understood without surrounding context?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.10 Section Headings
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.10 Section Headings (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.10 Section Headings (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
Section headings organize written content and help readers navigate long documents. This criterion concerns sections within writing, rather than the names of interactive components.
Implementation and testing
Introduce meaningful section headings and use semantic heading elements where appropriate. A heading should identify the section, not merely create large decorative text.
Real-world example: the barrier
A long policy is presented as one uninterrupted block. Readers cannot quickly find the sections about registration, payment or cancellation.
Improved design and verification
Organize the writing into meaningful sections with descriptive headings. Inspect the document heading outline and check that each heading describes its following section.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A long document contains several topics but no section headings.
Improved approach:

Eligibility

...

How to apply

...
Headings organize written sections and should describe the content that follows. Keep a meaningful hierarchy rather than choosing levels only for size.
Detailed guidance

Section headings help readers identify the organization of written material and jump to a relevant topic. A large wall of text requires more sustained reading and makes it harder to locate a particular step or policy.

Use headings for meaningful sections rather than inserting them solely to increase font size. Semantic heading elements can expose an outline to assistive technology; use levels that reflect the document structure. A heading should match the content that follows and avoid repeating the same vague word for unrelated sections.

This criterion concerns sections within writing, not the names of user interface components. Inspect a long article’s heading list independently of its body. Verify that the list conveys the article’s structure and that users can find the relevant section without reading every paragraph.
Worked verification

Take a long guide and divide it where its subject or task changes, such as eligibility, application steps, and appeals. Give each section a heading that previews the content below it. Use real heading semantics so a screen reader can expose the hierarchy. Then scan the headings without the body: a reader should be able to predict where to find a topic. Decorative bold text alone may not communicate the same structure.
Further explanation and testing

Section headings expose the organization of written content. They support people who scan before reading, readers who need to revisit a particular instruction, and screen reader users who navigate by headings. The criterion concerns headings that organize content; it does not mean every paragraph needs a heading or that larger text alone creates a useful structure.

Divide a long policy into meaningful sections such as eligibility, application steps, and appeals. Use a heading that accurately describes each section and apply semantic heading elements with levels that reflect the document hierarchy. Avoid choosing a heading level solely for its visual size; styling can be adjusted separately from structure.

Inspect the heading list without reading the body. Can a learner predict where to find a refund rule or a required document? Then read each section to verify that its heading remains accurate. Check nested sections, dynamically loaded content, and translated pages. Related criteria address whether headings and labels describe their purpose; this criterion focuses on providing headings that organize the content.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A long cancellation policy contains paragraphs about eligibility, refunds, and appeals but has no section headings. Add headings that describe those subjects, use appropriate semantic heading levels, and inspect the resulting outline. Ask a reader to find the appeal process using only the headings before checking the full text. A heading that says “More” for every section is not an effective navigation aid. Avoid introducing a heading solely to obtain a larger font when it does not represent a section.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Divide a long policy into sections headed “Eligibility,” “How to apply,” and “Appeals,” using semantic heading elements in a coherent hierarchy. Inspect the heading list separately from the page body, then verify that each heading accurately describes the following content. Styling a paragraph in bold can create a visual cue but may not expose the same structure to assistive technology. Conversely, using headings just for larger font can make the outline misleading. Test nested sections and translated versions as content changes.
Worked example and edge cases

A policy article presents registration, payment, refunds, and appeals as a single uninterrupted block. Divide the material into sections and provide headings that describe the topic of each section. Use real heading elements so users can navigate the document structure, and check that the heading hierarchy reflects the relationship between main topics and subsections. A heading should prepare the reader for what follows, not merely repeat a generic phrase such as “More.” Evaluate sections that were added through a content management system, where visually bold text may not have heading semantics.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Break a long help article into logical sections, add descriptive headings and inspect the resulting heading outline.
Knowledge check
What is the primary purpose of section headings here?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
At AA, an author-created overlay must not entirely hide a component that has keyboard focus. Sticky headers, footers and floating banners can cover focused controls.
Implementation and testing

Account for overlays when scrolling focus into view, for example with suitable scroll padding. Check at zoomed sizes and with keyboard navigation; the criterion addresses the focused component, not just its outline.
Real-world example: the barrier
A sticky footer completely covers a submit button after keyboard focus moves to it. The user can activate the hidden button without seeing where focus is.
Improved design and verification
Adjust scrolling or overlay placement so at least part of the focused component remains visible. Retest with zoom and different viewport heights.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A fixed footer completely covers a focused submit button.
Improved approach:
html { scroll-padding-bottom: 5rem; }
Scroll padding can help but must match the actual overlay and be tested in real layouts, especially when zoom changes available space.
Detailed guidance

Sticky headers, fixed footers, cookie notices and chat widgets occupy screen space that ordinary document flow may not reserve. When the browser scrolls a focused control into view, that control can land underneath an overlay. A user may hear the name of a control while being unable to see it, or may activate a control whose location is unclear.

The minimum criterion concerns whether the focused component is entirely hidden by author-created content. It does not mean the focus ring must be entirely visible, and it is not the same measurement as the enhanced AAA criterion, which prohibits any part of the component being hidden. Apply the criteria to the actual component and the layout that the user receives.

Reserve space or adjust scroll offsets for fixed regions. CSS scroll-padding can help browsers choose a better scroll position, but a hard-coded value that works on a wide screen may fail when a banner wraps at higher zoom. Check the actual overlay height, resize behavior and dynamic opening of notices. A CSS declaration by itself is not proof that the control is visible.

Start at the top of a long page and tab through every control near the bottom edge. Repeat with increased zoom, a narrow viewport and any author-provided notice open. Note whether the entire focused component is covered. When user-opened content can be dismissed or moved without advancing focus, account for the relevant criterion notes in the test.
Further explanation and testing

A component can receive keyboard focus while a sticky header, footer, banner, or chat panel covers it. The user may press Enter or type without seeing which element has focus. This AA criterion addresses a focused component that is entirely hidden by author-created content; the related AAA criterion requires the whole component to remain unobscured. The component and its focus indicator are related but separate things to inspect.

Reproduce the problem with a short viewport and at browser zoom. Tab to controls near a fixed header and footer, then examine whether any part of the focused component is visible. An overlay that only appears at a breakpoint or after a notification is opened can make the problem intermittent. Also check dynamically opened menus and the layout when a virtual keyboard reduces the available viewport.

Potential repairs include reserving space for fixed regions, repositioning them, or setting suitable scroll offsets. A fixed offset can fail when the banner text wraps, so test its actual height across screen sizes and translated content. Repeat the keyboard sequence after the fix, and ensure the remedy does not hide a different control. Record the viewport, zoom, overlay state, and focused element to make a failure reproducible.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: With a sticky footer visible, Tab to a submit button near the bottom of a form. If the entire button is hidden, change the layout or scroll positioning to expose it and repeat at a short viewport height. Test with the notification banner open as well as closed, because multiple overlays can combine. At this AA level inspect whether the component is entirely obscured; the enhanced criterion requires the whole component to remain visible. Check focus-indicator visibility as a related but separate requirement.
Implementation review

Implementation review: When focus lands on a button behind a sticky footer, adjust the layout or scrolling so the component is not entirely hidden. Test at a short viewport height, at zoom, and with optional banners open. A fixed scroll offset can fail if an overlay grows or wraps; inspect the actual rendered page. This AA criterion concerns a component entirely obscured by author-created content, while the enhanced criterion requires the whole component to remain visible. Test the focus indicator separately, because seeing part of a component does not necessarily make its indicator visible.
Worked example and edge cases

A sticky footer covers a focused Submit button completely when the user tabs to the bottom of a form. Move the footer, provide sufficient scroll offset, or otherwise ensure that the component is not entirely hidden by author-created content. Test the entire keyboard path, not just a manually scrolled screenshot: focus movement can trigger a different scroll position. Repeat at high zoom, with a small viewport, and when a cookie notice or other fixed region is present. This minimum criterion concerns complete obscuration of the focused component; the enhanced criterion requires a stronger outcome.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity

Knowledge check
A sticky banner fully covers the focused button. What is the relevant issue?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
The AAA enhanced requirement is stricter than 2.4.11: no part of the focused component may be hidden by author-created content.
Implementation and testing
Test scroll position near sticky headers and footers and account for varying viewport sizes. A partially visible button may satisfy the minimum requirement but still fail this enhanced one.
Real-world example: the barrier
A sticky header covers the upper half of a focused link. The link is not fully hidden, but its entire component is not visible.
Improved design and verification
Provide enough scroll offset or change the layout so the full focused component is visible. Test again at high zoom, where fixed regions can take up more space.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A focused control is partly hidden under a sticky banner.
Improved approach:
Reposition the banner or scroll until the entire focused component is visible.
The enhanced criterion evaluates every part of the component, not only whether some of it is visible.
Detailed guidance

The enhanced AAA focus-obscuration criterion requires that no part of a focused component be hidden by author-created content. This is stricter than the AA minimum, where the failure concerns a component that is entirely hidden.

Fixed headers, banners and floating widgets are common sources of partial coverage. At high zoom a banner may grow taller or wrap, so an offset that works at a normal viewport may no longer protect the whole control. Treat both horizontal and vertical clipping as layout questions to inspect.

Tab through controls near each fixed region and inspect the complete bounding area of the focused component. Adjust the layout or scrolling behavior so that the whole component is visible. Also verify the focus indicator itself under the applicable focus visibility requirements.
Worked verification

Test at several viewport heights and zoom levels, because a fixed banner that covers only a few pixels at one size can hide half a control at another. Focus each control near an overlay and inspect all edges of the component, not just its label or focus ring. Consider scroll margins, repositioning the overlay, or reducing fixed content. Retest after a banner wraps or the virtual keyboard changes the available viewport.
Further explanation and testing

A focused control can be partially covered by a fixed header, a cookie notice, or a floating panel. A person may see part of it but miss its label, value, or surrounding context. This AAA criterion requires that no part of the focused component be hidden by author-created content, a stricter standard than the AA condition addressing a component that is entirely hidden.

The problem can depend on viewport size, zoom, or content wrapping. A banner that is shallow on a wide screen may become tall when zoomed or translated. Provide sufficient layout space or adjust scrolling so the focused component remains fully visible. A hard-coded offset must be tested against the actual size of the overlay rather than assumed to work in every state.

Tab to controls near fixed regions at several viewport heights and zoom levels. Inspect all edges of the component, not only whether the focus indicator is visible. Test with notices expanded and collapsed and with a virtual keyboard where relevant. Confirm that a fix for one overlay does not cause another to cover the next focused control.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A sticky header covers the top half of a focused link. Although part of the link remains visible, this enhanced criterion requires the entire focused component to be unobscured by author-created content. Add layout space or a suitable scroll offset, then retest at high zoom and in a translated interface where the header wraps. Check both top and bottom overlays and the whole component boundary, not just the visible text. The fix should continue to work when a banner expands dynamically.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A fixed header that covers the top edge of a focused field creates a partial obstruction. Reserve adequate space or change the scroll positioning, then inspect all edges of the focused component. Repeat with zoom, a narrow viewport, translated header text, and a virtual keyboard when relevant. An offset chosen for a single header height may fail when the header wraps. This AAA requirement is stricter than the AA criterion that addresses a component entirely hidden. Verify that correcting the header does not leave the component covered by a footer instead.
Worked example and edge cases

A sticky header covers the top half of a focused link. Because the link is only partly hidden, the minimum requirement and this enhanced requirement have different outcomes. For the enhanced target, adjust scroll margins or overlay placement so the entire focused component remains visible. Check each edge of the component, not merely whether a few pixels of its focus indicator appear. Repeat when text wraps, the viewport becomes shorter, or the on-screen keyboard reduces available space. If several fixed regions can appear together, test their combined effect instead of reviewing each in isolation.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Focus a button partly underneath a sticky header. Adjust scrolling so the whole component remains visible and compare the AA and AAA outcomes.
Knowledge check
A focused button is partly covered by an author-created banner. What is the AAA concern?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.4.13 Focus Appearance
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

At AAA, a visible focus indicator must provide an area at least as large as a two-CSS-pixel-thick perimeter of the unfocused component and a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in focused and unfocused states, subject to defined exceptions.
Implementation and testing

A two-pixel outline is a useful starting point, not automatic proof: check its actual area and focused-versus-unfocused pixel contrast, including clipping and overlap. Exceptions cover certain unmodified user-agent indicators.
Real-world example: the barrier
A designer changes a button’s border by a barely perceptible color when it receives focus. The focused and unfocused appearances are hard to distinguish.
Improved design and verification
Measure the indicator area and compare the same pixels between states. Check the required perimeter-equivalent area and 3:1 change in contrast, subject to the stated exceptions.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A one-pixel focus change is almost indistinguishable from the unfocused state.
Improved approach:
Measure an indicator with area at least equivalent to a two-CSS-pixel perimeter and at least 3:1 change for the same pixels.
A sample two-pixel outline is only a starting point: clipping, color and the actual focused and unfocused backgrounds affect measurement.
Detailed guidance

A focus indicator needs enough visible change for users to distinguish focused and unfocused states. The AAA criterion measures an indicator area and a contrast change; it should not be reduced to a recommendation that every element use an arbitrary border.

The qualifying area must be at least the area of a two-CSS-pixel-thick perimeter of the unfocused component or subcomponent, and it must have at least 3:1 contrast between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states. The criterion has exceptions for certain user-agent-determined or author-unmodified indicators.

Measure the rendered component and indicator, accounting for clipping, overlaps and the state before focus. Compare the same pixels in both states; a color that contrasts with a neighboring background does not automatically prove the required state change. Test actual widgets and viewport conditions rather than assuming a CSS outline declaration is always sufficient.
Worked verification

Capture focused and unfocused states at the same scale, then compare the pixels occupied by the indicator between those states. The area and contrast-change requirements are distinct: a large indicator with too little state contrast is not sufficient, and a tiny high-contrast mark may not have sufficient area. Include clipping by neighboring elements in the inspection and account for the criterion’s exceptions before reporting a failure.
Further explanation and testing

An indicator that is technically present can still be too thin or too similar to the unfocused state to distinguish. The enhanced focus appearance criterion adds measurable requirements for the size of the indicator and the contrast change between focused and unfocused states, subject to stated exceptions. It is not enough to check whether a control has any outline property in CSS.

The qualifying area must be at least the area of a two-CSS-pixel-thick perimeter of the unfocused component or subcomponent, and the indicator must achieve a contrast change of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the two states. Distinguish this state comparison from the contrast between adjacent colors. A bright focus ring may contrast with its neighbor but still require checking against what occupied those same pixels before focus.

Measure the rendered component and compare focused and unfocused screenshots or use an appropriate inspection tool. Account for clipping, overlays, and parts of an indicator that are not visible. Inspect custom controls, different themes, and zoomed layouts. Check the specified exceptions for user-agent-determined or unmodified indicators rather than assuming all browser defaults are handled identically.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A button uses a thin blue border in both states, changing only to a slightly darker blue on focus. Capture the same area before and after focus. Check whether enough pixels meet the required 3:1 state-change contrast and whether their area meets the two-pixel-perimeter equivalent. A border that contrasts against the page background is not necessarily sufficient if it barely changes on focus. Inspect clipping and overlapping elements, and assess the criterion’s exceptions before reporting the result.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Capture a control before and after focus at the same scale. Determine the area of pixels constituting the focus indicator and compare the same pixels across the two states for the required 3:1 change. The qualifying area must meet the two-CSS-pixel-perimeter equivalent described by the criterion. Contrast with a neighboring background is a different measurement and does not automatically prove state-change contrast. Include clipping and overlap in the inspection, and evaluate applicable exceptions for user-agent-determined or author-unmodified indicators. Test representative component shapes and themes.
Worked example and edge cases

A button changes its border from light gray to slightly darker gray when focused. Evaluate both the indicator's area and the contrast change between the focused and unfocused states at the same pixels. A high-contrast one-pixel dot may be too small, while a broad subtle outline may not provide enough contrast change. Compare the measured area with the area of a two CSS-pixel-thick perimeter of the unfocused component and check the specified 3:1 change, taking the criterion's exceptions into account. Inspect screenshots at the same scale and ensure the indicator is not clipped by a neighboring container.
Planning a thorough review

Navigation testing should follow an actual task. Start at a realistic entry point, such as a search result or the browser address bar, and identify how a user finds the page, understands its purpose, reaches the relevant section, and moves among controls. Check both the visible interface and programmatically available structure: browser titles, heading elements, links, landmarks, and focus order may communicate different parts of the experience. Use a screen reader or accessibility tree inspection to verify names and structure, then perform a separate keyboard pass to observe focus and navigation.

Repeat the check after client-side route changes and at a narrow viewport or high zoom. Sticky headers, responsive reordering, hidden menus, and dynamically inserted content can change the result. Record the exact starting point and actions, the expected destination or focus location, and what actually happened. Fixing one cue does not automatically fix another: a descriptive page title does not create a bypass link, and an on-screen label does not guarantee that focus remains visible. Evaluate the particular condition and level in the lesson before deciding whether the observed behavior passes.
Required practical activity
Measure a button’s indicator area and compare the same pixels before and after focus. Record whether it reaches both thresholds.
Knowledge check
Which measurements are relevant to Focus Appearance?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

Multipoint or path-based gestures must have a single-pointer alternative that does not require a path-based gesture, unless the gesture is essential. This helps users who cannot pinch or trace a precise path.
Implementation and testing

Offer plus and minus buttons for a pinch-to-zoom map and separate previous/next buttons for a swipe carousel. A simple pointer alternative is different from keyboard support, though both may be needed.
Real-world example: the barrier
A photo viewer changes images only when a user swipes horizontally. A user operating a pointer with limited precision cannot perform the gesture reliably.
Improved design and verification
Add previous and next buttons that work with a single tap. Verify that they expose the same images and do not require tracing a particular path.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A map can zoom only through a pinch gesture.
Improved approach:
<button type="button" aria-label="Zoom in">+</button>
Connect the button to the same zoom operation and offer zoom out as well. A tap avoids a multipoint or path-based gesture.
Detailed guidance

A multipoint gesture uses more than one point of contact, such as pinching a map. A path-based gesture depends on moving through a particular path, such as swiping a carousel or tracing a shape. Some users can tap but cannot reliably coordinate multiple fingers or maintain a precise movement, particularly when using a head pointer or other pointing aid.

Provide the same function through a single pointer without requiring a path-based gesture, unless that gesture is essential. For a map, plus and minus buttons can offer the same zoom operation. For a gallery, previous and next buttons can show the same set of images. Merely adding an explanation of the swipe does not supply an alternative operation.

Separate the gesture requirements from keyboard requirements. A keyboard shortcut can be a valuable additional method but it does not by itself offer a single-pointer alternative. Conversely, a tap-operated button should still be made keyboard accessible when other applicable criteria require it. Check labels, target size and pointer cancellation in addition to the gesture itself.

Test with a mouse or one finger: without dragging, swiping or using a second contact point, perform every action that the gesture offers. Compare the outcomes and range of available values. If the gesture is asserted to be essential, explain why the underlying function cannot be achieved another way rather than treating the existing implementation as the definition of the task.
Further explanation and testing

A multipoint gesture requires more than one point of contact, such as a two-finger pinch. A path-based gesture depends on the path followed, such as a swipe. Some users cannot maintain multiple contacts or move a pointer along a particular route, even if they can activate a single target. This criterion generally requires an alternative that can be operated by a single pointer without a path, unless the gesture is essential.

In an image gallery, previous and next buttons can provide the same navigation as a swipe. In a map, zoom buttons can provide an alternative to pinching, though the team must also examine other map operations independently. Make the controls visible, label their purpose, and ensure they produce the same relevant result. A keyboard alternative may help another group of users, but it does not by itself establish that a single-pointer alternative is available.

Test using taps or clicks without dragging, pinching, or tracing a route. Start from the same state, use the gesture and the alternative separately, and compare the outcomes. Verify boundaries, such as the first and last gallery image, and make sure the available control is not hidden behind a gesture. Distinguish path-based gestures from ordinary dragging, which is addressed separately by 2.5.7.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A gallery changes photos by swiping, but its arrow controls are decorative and do not respond to a tap. Convert them into operable previous and next buttons and verify they reach the same images as the swipe. Test with a single pointer without tracing a path. For a pinch-to-zoom image, zoom buttons can offer another route to magnification. A keyboard-only workaround can help some users but does not replace the required single-pointer alternative when this criterion applies.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A gallery with swipe navigation can provide native Previous and Next buttons. Tap each button with a single pointer and confirm it reaches the same images as the swipe. For pinch zoom, plus and minus controls can expose magnification without a multipoint gesture; assess other operations independently. A button reachable only through a keyboard shortcut does not provide the required single-pointer alternative. If a path or multipoint gesture is claimed to be essential, explain why the underlying function cannot be performed through an alternative rather than relying on the original design choice.
Worked example and edge cases

A gallery moves between photographs only when the user swipes across the image. Provide Previous and Next controls that can be activated with a single pointer action without tracing a path. Verify that the buttons reach every photograph available through swiping and that their state communicates when an endpoint is reached. Multi-point gestures and path-based gestures are covered by this requirement unless the gesture is essential. Keyboard support remains valuable but does not by itself supply the single-pointer alternative required here. Test with a mouse, touch, and another pointer input where available.
Planning a thorough review

Evaluate the pointer task from the user's perspective, from the initial contact through the final result. Identify whether the design requires a path, multiple contact points, dragging, a down-event, precise targeting, or movement of the device. Those are distinct interaction characteristics, and each has its own requirements and exceptions. Check that an alternative completes the same underlying operation, including any selection, confirmation, and error recovery; an alternative that opens a menu but cannot finish the task is incomplete.

Test the actual interactive region rather than only the visible icon. Use browser tools to inspect CSS-pixel dimensions and boundaries, then try adjacent targets with a mouse or touch. For cancellation, press and hold, move away, and release using sample data, and verify whether a server-side action occurred. For accessible naming, compare visible text with the computed name and repeat after localization or state changes. Keyboard access is important, but a keyboard-only workaround does not automatically meet a requirement for an alternative operable by a single pointer.
Required practical activity
Test a swipe-only gallery using a single tap. Add and test a previous and next control.
Knowledge check
What alternative can make a pinch-to-zoom map usable with a single pointer?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

A pointer action that completes on press can be triggered accidentally before a user can move away. The criterion offers several ways to prevent or reverse unintended activation, with an essential-function exception.
Implementation and testing

For ordinary buttons, complete the action on release and permit the user to move away before release. Alternatively provide an appropriate undo, an up-event reversal, or meet another specified condition.
Real-world example: the barrier
An order is canceled as soon as the pointer touches the cancel control. An accidental press leaves no chance to move away or undo.
Improved design and verification
Complete the action on release while allowing the user to abort before release, or use another allowed cancellation mechanism. Test both press-and-move-away and normal activation.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A destructive function runs on pointerdown with no abort or undo.
Improved approach:
Complete on pointerup with a way to abort before completion, or provide an applicable undo.
Test press, move away, then release. Standard click behavior can help, but actual event handlers must not trigger the action earlier.
Detailed guidance

When an action completes on the down event, a person who touches the wrong control may have no opportunity to correct the mistake. Completing an ordinary operation on release can let the user move away before releasing, preventing accidental activation.

The criterion provides multiple alternatives, including not using the down event to execute any part of the function, completing on up with an abort or undo mechanism, reversing the down-event outcome on up, or an essential-function exception. Evaluate the complete behavior; merely adding a click listener is not enough if a separate pointerdown handler already performs the destructive action.

Press and hold the control, move away and release; verify the resulting action. Then activate normally and test any undo. Consider touch, mouse and assistive pointing devices. Some controls that emulate a keyboard or numeric keypad press have an essential-operation note, so inspect the specific function rather than assuming every press must work identically.
Worked verification

Reproduce an accidental press by pressing a control, holding, moving the pointer outside it, and releasing. Observe whether the action still occurs. For an action completed on release, provide an abort or undo as specified by the criterion; if the action already happens on pointer down, check whether release reverses it or another permitted condition applies. Test destructive actions with reversible sample data so the behavior can be observed without harming real records.
Further explanation and testing

Pointer cancellation helps prevent accidental activation when someone presses the wrong target. An action performed immediately on pointer down can leave no opportunity to move away before committing it. This is especially consequential for deletion, cancellation, and purchases, but even a less serious action can disrupt a person’s task.

The criterion provides several permitted approaches: no part of the function is executed on the down event; the action completes on up and there is a mechanism to abort before completion or undo afterward; the up event reverses the down-event outcome; or completing on down is essential. Evaluate the actual event handling. A click handler does not help if another pointerdown handler has already carried out the irreversible operation.

With safe sample data, press and hold the target, move outside it, and release. Observe whether the action is aborted or whether an available undo restores the previous state. Then perform a normal activation and verify its result. Test touch and mouse where supported, and inspect the essential-function exception in the context of the actual control rather than assuming it applies to all buttons.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A user presses a Delete button, notices the mistake, moves the pointer away, and releases. The record should not be deleted if the chosen design uses release with an abort mechanism. If the action is performed on pointer down, examine whether the up event reverses it or another permitted condition applies. Test using disposable sample records. A visually displayed Undo control is not sufficient unless it actually restores the affected data after normal activation.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Use a normal release-based activation for a destructive action and allow the user to move away before release, or provide another mechanism permitted by the criterion. Test by pressing, holding, moving outside, and releasing over safe sample data. Then activate normally and test any Undo. Inspect pointerdown handlers as well as click handlers: an early deletion cannot be cured by an unrelated release handler unless the criterion’s conditions are actually met. Consider the essential exception in relation to the specific operation, not all controls in a class.
Worked example and edge cases

A delete control performs the deletion immediately on pointer down. To examine accidental activation, press the control, hold the pointer down, move outside the target, and release. A design that completes on release can allow the user to abort before completion or undo afterward, in line with the criterion's options. Check actual business effects as well as the visual button state: a server request fired on pointer down can delete the item even if the interface later looks canceled. Use reversible sample records during testing. Also distinguish a justified essential down-event from a developer's convenience.
Planning a thorough review

Evaluate the pointer task from the user's perspective, from the initial contact through the final result. Identify whether the design requires a path, multiple contact points, dragging, a down-event, precise targeting, or movement of the device. Those are distinct interaction characteristics, and each has its own requirements and exceptions. Check that an alternative completes the same underlying operation, including any selection, confirmation, and error recovery; an alternative that opens a menu but cannot finish the task is incomplete.

Test the actual interactive region rather than only the visible icon. Use browser tools to inspect CSS-pixel dimensions and boundaries, then try adjacent targets with a mouse or touch. For cancellation, press and hold, move away, and release using sample data, and verify whether a server-side action occurred. For accessible naming, compare visible text with the computed name and repeat after localization or state changes. Keyboard access is important, but a keyboard-only workaround does not automatically meet a requirement for an alternative operable by a single pointer.
Required practical activity
Press and hold a delete button, move the pointer away, then release. Confirm whether the delete is canceled and whether an undo is available.
Knowledge check
How can a normal delete button support pointer cancellation?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.5.3 Label in Name
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem
For controls with a visible text label, the accessible name must contain that visible text. Speech users often activate a control by saying the words they can see.
Implementation and testing

Prefer the visible wording at the beginning of the accessible name. If a button says “Search”, an aria-label of “Find items” alone can make voice activation unpredictable; test the computed accessible name.
Real-world example: the barrier
A button visibly says “Search”, but an overriding accessible name says “Find items”. A voice user says the visible word and cannot reliably activate the control.
Improved design and verification
Include the visible word in the computed name, preferably at the start, such as “Search products”. Inspect the accessibility tree and test a voice command.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
<button aria-label="Find items">Search</button>
Improved approach:
<button aria-label="Search products">Search</button>
The computed accessible name now includes the visible label. Verify it in the accessibility tree and test a speech command.
Detailed guidance

Speech input users often identify an on-screen control by speaking its visible label. If an author overrides its accessible name with unrelated words, the command may not match what the user sees. This mismatch can also make collaboration between sighted and assistive-technology users confusing.

For a control with a visible text label or image of text, ensure that its accessible name contains that visible text. A useful convention is to place the visible text at the beginning, followed by clarifying information where needed. For example, “Search products” contains the visible label “Search”.

Inspect the computed accessible name, including any aria-label or aria-labelledby that overrides text content. Compare the visible text and the announced name and try a voice command using the visible wording. Do not assume that a visually obvious icon supplies the same name to assistive technology.
Worked verification

Inspect the computed accessible name in browser developer tools, because aria-label or aria-labelledby can replace what is announced. If a button displays “Send” but is named “Submit message,” a speech user may say the visible word and fail to activate it. “Send message” preserves the visible wording and adds context. Repeat the comparison after localization and when labels change dynamically, not only in the default language and state.
Further explanation and testing

A person using speech input often tries to activate a control by saying its visible label. If its accessible name uses different words, the command may fail even though the control looks correct. The visible and programmatic names also matter when one person helps another navigate a page using the words displayed on screen.

For an interface component with a visible text label or image of text, the accessible name must contain the visible text. Place that text at the beginning when practical, followed by useful context. For example, a button visibly labeled “Search” might have the accessible name “Search products.” Be careful when adding aria-label or aria-labelledby, because these attributes can override the name that would otherwise come from the button’s text.

Inspect the computed accessible name rather than assuming it matches the markup. Compare it with the text visible on screen, and try invoking the control using that wording with speech software where available. Repeat for translated labels, icon buttons with visible text, and states in which a label changes. A descriptive accessible name that omits the visible words can still create a speech-input barrier.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A visible button says “Search,” but aria-label gives it the accessible name “Find products.” Inspect the computed name, then change it to include “Search,” for example “Search products.” A speech user should be able to identify the control using the visible wording. Repeat after switching languages and after the button label changes during a loading state. Avoid hiding necessary visible label words inside unrelated programmatic names, even if those names sound descriptive in isolation.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A visible “Search” button with aria-label="Find products" can be hard to activate by speech using the visible word. Give it an accessible name containing the visible text, such as “Search products,” and inspect the computed name in browser tools. Test after translation and when the visible label changes. Avoid accidentally overriding meaningful button text with an unrelated aria-label or aria-labelledby reference. The visible wording at the beginning of the accessible name is a helpful convention; the requirement is that the accessible name contains the visible label under the criterion’s conditions.
Worked example and edge cases

A visible button says “Search” but an aria-label overrides its accessible name to “Find products.” A speech-input user may say the visible word and be unable to target the control reliably. Include the visible text in the accessible name, preferably at the start, such as “Search products.” Inspect the computed name rather than assuming the markup combines labels as intended. Repeat after translation and when the button changes state. A longer name can add context, but replacing the visible words with a synonym defeats the connection between what a user sees and what the assistive technology can target.
Planning a thorough review

Evaluate the pointer task from the user's perspective, from the initial contact through the final result. Identify whether the design requires a path, multiple contact points, dragging, a down-event, precise targeting, or movement of the device. Those are distinct interaction characteristics, and each has its own requirements and exceptions. Check that an alternative completes the same underlying operation, including any selection, confirmation, and error recovery; an alternative that opens a menu but cannot finish the task is incomplete.

Test the actual interactive region rather than only the visible icon. Use browser tools to inspect CSS-pixel dimensions and boundaries, then try adjacent targets with a mouse or touch. For cancellation, press and hold, move away, and release using sample data, and verify whether a server-side action occurred. For accessible naming, compare visible text with the computed name and repeat after localization or state changes. Keyboard access is important, but a keyboard-only workaround does not automatically meet a requirement for an alternative operable by a single pointer.
Required practical activity
Inspect a button labeled “Search” whose aria-label is “Find items”. Change its name to include the visible label and verify it in accessibility tools.
Knowledge check
A button visibly says “Search”. Which accessible name includes its visible label?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.5.4 Motion Actuation
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.5.4 Motion Actuation (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.5.4 Motion Actuation (Level A), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

When functionality is activated by moving a device or making a user motion, users generally need an alternative interface control and a way to disable motion activation. Supported-interface and essential-function exceptions are defined.
Implementation and testing
Provide a conventional undo button alongside shake-to-undo and let users turn shake activation off. Test accidental movement and ensure disabling motion does not remove the alternative.
Real-world example: the barrier
A mobile application undoes changes when the device is shaken, with no visible undo control and no way to turn off shake detection.
Improved design and verification
Add an undo button and a setting to disable shake activation. Test that normal movement cannot accidentally trigger the feature when it is disabled.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
Shake device to undo, with no alternative or setting.
Improved approach:
Provide an Undo button and a setting that disables shake activation.
The interface alternative and disable control address different barriers. Test both, unless a stated exception applies.
Detailed guidance

A feature may respond to motion of a device, such as shaking a phone, or motion of a user, such as a gesture detected by a camera. Some users cannot perform the motion, while others may trigger it accidentally during ordinary movement.

Provide an alternative user interface component and let users disable responding to the motion, unless an applicable supported-interface or essential exception applies. A conventional Undo button can accompany shake-to-undo, and a preference can turn shake detection off. These address different needs: accessibility of the operation and prevention of accidental activation.

Test the alternative without moving the device and test that disabling motion prevents accidental activation. Review whether the claimed exception actually applies; a motion that is merely convenient or entertaining is not necessarily essential to the task.
Worked verification

Exercise both parts of the solution independently. First perform the task using the visible control without moving the device or user’s body. Then turn off motion activation and confirm that shaking or the monitored gesture no longer triggers the action accidentally. If claiming that movement is essential or supported through an accessibility interface, document why the actual feature qualifies rather than assuming all motion features are exempt.
Further explanation and testing

Some interfaces perform actions when a device is moved or when a person makes a motion detected by a sensor. Examples include shaking a phone to undo or using a camera-detected gesture. Someone may be unable to perform the motion, while another person may trigger it unintentionally during ordinary movement.

Provide an alternative user-interface component for the operation and let the user disable motion response, except where an applicable supported-interface or essential exception applies. For shake-to-undo, a visible Undo button offers another way to perform the action; a preference to turn off shake detection addresses accidental triggers. These are separate needs, so adding only one of the two may leave a barrier.

Perform the same operation without moving the device, then disable motion activation and check that ordinary movement no longer invokes it. Verify the preference can itself be reached and operated. Consider whether motion is genuinely essential to the function or whether it is simply a convenient shortcut. Document the reason when relying on an exception.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Shaking a phone undoes the last action. Add an Undo button and a preference to turn off the shake response. With motion disabled, shake the phone and confirm nothing is undone; then use the button and verify that it performs the same undo. Check that the preference is accessible without shaking. If the team claims movement is essential, ask what function would be impossible through an alternative control and record the justification for the actual feature.
Implementation review

Implementation review: For shake-to-undo, provide an Undo button and a setting that disables the shake response. Use the button without moving the device and verify that it undoes the same operation. Then disable the motion response, shake the device, and confirm no accidental undo occurs. Both tests matter because the alternative control and the ability to disable motion address different barriers. Evaluate the supported-interface and essential exceptions against the actual feature. A motion gesture that is merely fun or convenient is not automatically essential.
Worked example and edge cases

A mobile app clears a form when the device is shaken. Give users another interface control for the same function and let them disable motion actuation, unless an applicable exception is met. Test those protections separately: perform the operation without moving the device, then disable motion and confirm that shaking no longer triggers it. Consider accidental movements while a user is walking or using a mobility aid. A label in help documentation does not replace the alternative control or disable setting. Document the basis for any essential-function or accessibility-interface exception rather than assuming all sensor input qualifies.
Planning a thorough review

Evaluate the pointer task from the user's perspective, from the initial contact through the final result. Identify whether the design requires a path, multiple contact points, dragging, a down-event, precise targeting, or movement of the device. Those are distinct interaction characteristics, and each has its own requirements and exceptions. Check that an alternative completes the same underlying operation, including any selection, confirmation, and error recovery; an alternative that opens a menu but cannot finish the task is incomplete.

Test the actual interactive region rather than only the visible icon. Use browser tools to inspect CSS-pixel dimensions and boundaries, then try adjacent targets with a mouse or touch. For cancellation, press and hold, move away, and release using sample data, and verify whether a server-side action occurred. For accessible naming, compare visible text with the computed name and repeat after localization or state changes. Keyboard access is important, but a keyboard-only workaround does not automatically meet a requirement for an alternative operable by a single pointer.
Required practical activity
Review a shake-to-undo feature. Add a visible undo control and a setting that disables shake activation.
Knowledge check
How should a nonessential shake-to-undo feature be made more accessible?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.
