lessons.title: 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced)
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

The AAA enhanced target-size criterion generally requires pointer targets to be at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, with defined exceptions including equivalent controls, inline targets, unmodified user-agent controls and essential presentation.
Implementation and testing
Measure the interactive hit area in CSS pixels, not just the icon graphic. Consider both dimensions and test adjacent controls on touch devices; spacing alone is not the general AAA size rule.
Real-world example: the barrier
A toolbar displays 16-pixel icons with equally tiny clickable regions. A user with limited pointer accuracy repeatedly activates the wrong item.
Improved design and verification
Expand each actual target to at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels unless an applicable exception is met. Keep the icon visually smaller if desired and verify the hit area.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
An icon button has a 16-by-16 CSS-pixel hit area.
Improved approach:
button.icon { min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px; }
The rendered hit area must meet both dimensions unless an exception applies. Check layout and target overlap on the actual device.
Detailed guidance

The enhanced AAA target-size criterion generally requires pointer targets to be at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels. The target is the clickable or tappable area, which may be larger than the visual icon. This larger area helps people who have difficulty making precise movements.

The criterion includes specific exceptions, including an equivalent target on the same page, inline targets, unmodified user-agent controls and essential presentation. The AA minimum-size criterion has its own requirements and exceptions; do not assume its spacing exception automatically satisfies this AAA criterion.

Inspect the actual rendered hit area using browser tools and try activating adjacent controls on a touch device. Enlarging padding can improve the target without enlarging the icon, but check that nearby controls do not overlap and that layout remains usable at zoom.
Worked verification

Measure the interactive hit area in CSS pixels, including padding, rather than measuring only the painted icon. Check adjacent targets at normal size and zoom: a large invisible target that overlaps a neighbor can create a different activation problem. If relying on an exception, identify its precise conditions and test the proposed equivalent target. The smaller minimum-size requirement and its spacing exception should not be substituted for this enhanced target.
Further explanation and testing

A target is the interactive area that responds to pointer input. An icon may look small while its surrounding clickable area is larger, so assess the actual hit area rather than only the painted graphic. The enhanced AAA criterion generally requires a target of at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, subject to its specified exceptions.

Larger targets help users whose pointer movement is imprecise and reduce accidental activation of neighboring controls. Padding can enlarge a button without changing the apparent size of its icon, but ensure that neighboring hit areas do not overlap. Review the actual layout when text wraps or the interface is zoomed. Do not substitute the spacing exception from the AA minimum-target criterion for an exception in this enhanced criterion.

Measure each target with browser tools and activate it near its edges with a pointer or touch device. Check closely spaced toolbar controls and links in prose separately because the criterion includes an inline exception with specific conditions. If relying on an equivalent target, verify that it is on the same page and provides the same function under the criterion’s conditions.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A toolbar icon is 16 by 16 CSS pixels, but its button has padding that makes the target 44 by 44. Measure the actual hit area, not just the icon. Verify that adjacent targets do not overlap and that the toolbar remains usable at zoom. An inline link within a sentence may be subject to a specific exception; a standalone toolbar button should not be assumed to qualify for the same reason. Also distinguish the enhanced criterion’s exceptions from the smaller AA minimum-size criterion.
Implementation review

Implementation review: An icon can remain visually 16 by 16 CSS pixels while padding gives its button a 44 by 44 CSS pixel hit area. Measure the interactive region and test activation at its edges; do not measure only the graphic. Check neighboring targets for overlaps and test at zoom. If the target is smaller, examine the specific enhanced-criterion exceptions, such as an eligible equivalent target or inline presentation, rather than borrowing the AA spacing exception. Record which exception applies and verify its conditions on the actual page.
Worked example and edge cases

A toolbar shows a sixteen-pixel icon, but its clickable button includes padding and measures forty-four by forty-four CSS pixels. Measure the interactive area, not just the artwork. Check adjacent controls so enlarged hit areas do not overlap or direct an activation to the wrong action. The enhanced criterion requires a target capable of containing a 44 by 44 CSS-pixel square, subject to its listed exceptions. Test zoom, responsive layouts, and controls inside embedded components. Do not substitute the smaller target and spacing rules of the minimum criterion for this enhanced target.
Planning a thorough review

Evaluate the pointer task from the user's perspective, from the initial contact through the final result. Identify whether the design requires a path, multiple contact points, dragging, a down-event, precise targeting, or movement of the device. Those are distinct interaction characteristics, and each has its own requirements and exceptions. Check that an alternative completes the same underlying operation, including any selection, confirmation, and error recovery; an alternative that opens a menu but cannot finish the task is incomplete.

Test the actual interactive region rather than only the visible icon. Use browser tools to inspect CSS-pixel dimensions and boundaries, then try adjacent targets with a mouse or touch. For cancellation, press and hold, move away, and release using sample data, and verify whether a server-side action occurred. For accessible naming, compare visible text with the computed name and repeat after localization or state changes. Keyboard access is important, but a keyboard-only workaround does not automatically meet a requirement for an alternative operable by a single pointer.
Required practical activity
Measure a toolbar button’s hit area and increase it to 44 by 44 CSS pixels without changing the icon size. Review whether any exception applies.
Knowledge check
What is the general AAA minimum pointer target size?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.5.6 Concurrent Input Mechanisms
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.5.6 Concurrent Input Mechanisms (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.5.6 Concurrent Input Mechanisms (Level AAA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

Users may switch between touch, keyboard, pointer and assistive inputs on the same device. At AAA, content must not restrict platform input modalities except where essential, needed for security, or required by user settings.
Implementation and testing
Avoid disabling keyboard controls merely because touch is detected. Test a hybrid laptop with both touch and keyboard during the same session and respect the user’s settings.
Real-world example: the barrier
A tablet app detects touch on startup and disables keyboard handlers for the rest of the session. A user who alternates between touch and a hardware keyboard loses access.
Improved design and verification
Keep available modalities usable together unless a specified exception applies. Test switching from touch to keyboard and back without reloading.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A touch-start handler disables keyboard navigation for the whole session.
Improved approach:
Keep touch, pointer and keyboard handlers available together.
A user may change inputs mid-task. Test on a hybrid device and distinguish restrictions required by security or user settings from developer convenience.
Detailed guidance

Many devices support several input methods at once. A person may use a touchscreen for broad navigation, a hardware keyboard for text, and a pointing device for a precision task. A site that chooses one mode at startup can prevent the user from changing methods when their circumstances change.

At AAA, content does not restrict platform input modalities except where restriction is essential, needed for content security, or required by user settings. Touch detection should generally enable touch support without disabling keyboard or mouse handling. Respect explicit user settings and assess genuine security restrictions separately.

Test on a hybrid device in one continuous session: activate a menu by touch, enter text by keyboard and use a pointer on another control. Confirm that switching does not require reloading and does not erase the current task. Check both author scripts and any third-party widgets.
Worked verification

On a convertible device, begin a task using touch, continue by keyboard, and finish with a mouse or trackpad without reloading. Check that touch detection has not removed keyboard focus or disabled pointer events. Repeat in embedded widgets, which may use separate event handling. An author may need a restriction for an essential function, security, or user settings, but a device being touch-capable alone is not such a reason.
Further explanation and testing

Modern devices often support more than one input method at the same time. A person may use touch for large targets, a keyboard to enter text, and a mouse for precise placement. An interface that detects a touchscreen and disables keyboard or mouse handling can prevent the user from switching methods as their needs or task change.

The enhanced concurrent-input criterion says content must not restrict available platform input modalities except where a restriction is essential, necessary for content security, or required to respect user settings. Supporting touch should ordinarily add an input option rather than replacing other available methods. Review application scripts and embedded components because either can impose an unexpected restriction.

On a hybrid device, start a task by touch, enter information with a keyboard, and use a pointer for the next control without reloading. Verify that focus, entered values, and state are retained. Then switch in the other direction. If a restriction is claimed to be essential or security-related, document the specific function and reason instead of relying on the fact that the device has a touchscreen.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: On a laptop with a touchscreen, open a menu by touch, enter text using the keyboard, and select another control with a trackpad. The task should continue without reloading or losing input because the first interaction was touch. Inspect third-party widgets if the rest of the page supports switching but one component does not. Review any security or user-setting restriction against the specific exception instead of treating touchscreen detection itself as a reason to disable keyboard support.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Do not disable keyboard event handling merely because a touchscreen is detected. On a hybrid device, open a menu by touch, enter text with a keyboard, and activate another control with a pointer during the same task. Confirm focus and entered data are retained when switching. Repeat in embedded widgets, which may use different input handling. If the product restricts a modality for an essential function, security, or a user setting, document the specific reason and verify that the restriction is limited to that case.
Worked example and edge cases

A tablet application detects touch at startup and disables keyboard event handlers. A user who begins with touch and then connects a keyboard cannot finish the task. Remove the restriction and test transitions among touch, keyboard, mouse, and available assistive input without reloading. Inspect embedded widgets separately because they may apply their own modality detection. The criterion permits restrictions when essential, required for security, or necessary to respect user settings; merely detecting a touch-capable screen is not enough. Document the actual reason for any restriction and check that other available inputs continue to work elsewhere.
Planning a thorough review

Evaluate the pointer task from the user's perspective, from the initial contact through the final result. Identify whether the design requires a path, multiple contact points, dragging, a down-event, precise targeting, or movement of the device. Those are distinct interaction characteristics, and each has its own requirements and exceptions. Check that an alternative completes the same underlying operation, including any selection, confirmation, and error recovery; an alternative that opens a menu but cannot finish the task is incomplete.

Test the actual interactive region rather than only the visible icon. Use browser tools to inspect CSS-pixel dimensions and boundaries, then try adjacent targets with a mouse or touch. For cancellation, press and hold, move away, and release using sample data, and verify whether a server-side action occurred. For accessible naming, compare visible text with the computed name and repeat after localization or state changes. Keyboard access is important, but a keyboard-only workaround does not automatically meet a requirement for an alternative operable by a single pointer.
Required practical activity
On a hybrid device, operate a menu by touch and then by keyboard without reloading. Record any modality that becomes unavailable.
Knowledge check
What is a suitable design for a touch-enabled laptop?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.5.7 Dragging Movements
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

A dragging movement needs a single-pointer alternative that does not require dragging, unless dragging is essential or is unmodified user-agent functionality. Keyboard support alone does not satisfy this pointer-specific requirement.
Implementation and testing
For sortable cards, add a menu with Move up and Move down actions. For sliders, offer tap controls or a numeric entry where appropriate, while preserving the underlying operation.
Real-world example: the barrier
A task board moves cards between columns only by dragging. A user can tap accurately but cannot sustain and steer a drag.
Improved design and verification
Add a tap-operated move menu that reaches every destination. Check that the action has the same result as dragging and remains available independently of keyboard support.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
A card can be moved only through drag-and-drop.
Improved approach:
Provide a Move menu with tap-operated destination choices.
Keyboard operation is valuable, but it does not replace the single-pointer alternative required for dragging movements.
Detailed guidance

Dragging requires a user to press, move while maintaining contact and release at an intended position. This can be difficult when a user has tremor, limited dexterity, an imprecise pointer or a device that cannot conveniently maintain a drag. A board may seem usable because its cards are visible and clickable, yet moving them may still be impossible.

The criterion requires functionality that uses dragging to be achievable with a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the functionality is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author. A menu of destination columns, a move-up and move-down control, or a click-source then click-destination workflow can provide an alternative. It must support the same meaningful result.

Do not confuse this with keyboard access. A reorderable list with excellent arrow-key support can still lack the required non-dragging pointer operation. Similarly, a tap control that only moves an item one position when dragging supports arbitrary destinations should be evaluated for whether users can actually reach all the same destinations through repeated operations.

Test the full task using a mouse or touch pointer without holding a button while moving. Move an item to the first, last and an intermediate position; confirm that the new order is saved and communicated. Repeat after errors or when an item cannot be moved. Keep any feedback understandable without relying solely on animation.
Further explanation and testing

Dragging requires a user to press, hold, move to a destination, and release while maintaining control. Someone may be able to tap an item and a destination but have difficulty sustaining a drag or moving precisely. The criterion requires a single-pointer operation without dragging for functionality that uses dragging, unless dragging is essential or the function is controlled by the user agent and not modified by the author.

For a task board, add a Move button or menu on each card. Present the possible destination columns, allow the person to select one by tapping, and give clear feedback after the card moves. If users can reorder within a column by dragging, the alternative must also address that operation; moving between columns alone does not cover reordering. Keyboard support is valuable but is not a substitute for a non-dragging single-pointer method.

Compare the complete operations offered by dragging with the operations offered by the alternative. Use taps to move a card, change its position where supported, and undo or correct a mistake if the application provides that feature. Test touch and mouse without holding down the pointer while moving. Ensure feedback identifies the destination and that the moved item remains discoverable in its new location.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: A task board allows a card to be dragged between columns and reordered within a column. Add a single-pointer Move menu and include both the destination and position controls necessary to reproduce those operations. Tap through the alternative without holding and moving the pointer. Compare the final state with the drag result, including any status announcements. Arrow-key support is valuable for keyboard users, but it does not by itself provide a non-dragging single-pointer operation.
Implementation review

Implementation review: A draggable task card can also expose a Move menu with choices for destination and position. Tap the card’s menu, select a column, and choose an ordering position without holding and moving a pointer. Compare the result with the drag workflow. If dragging permits reordering but the menu only changes columns, the alternative covers only part of the functionality. Keyboard commands are useful but do not replace the single-pointer non-dragging operation. Inspect whether any essential or user-agent-controlled exception applies to the particular functionality.
Worked example and edge cases

A task board lets users move cards only by dragging. Add a Move menu that allows a user to select the destination column with individual pointer activations, without holding and steering the card. Verify that the alternative can reach every destination and preserves the same result, including ordering if ordering is part of the operation. Keyboard shortcuts are useful but do not alone provide a single-pointer alternative. Test the menu with touch and a mouse, and inspect whether authorization or validation rules are consistent with the drag path. The criterion has exceptions for essential dragging and functionality determined by the user agent.
Planning a thorough review

Evaluate the pointer task from the user's perspective, from the initial contact through the final result. Identify whether the design requires a path, multiple contact points, dragging, a down-event, precise targeting, or movement of the device. Those are distinct interaction characteristics, and each has its own requirements and exceptions. Check that an alternative completes the same underlying operation, including any selection, confirmation, and error recovery; an alternative that opens a menu but cannot finish the task is incomplete.

Test the actual interactive region rather than only the visible icon. Use browser tools to inspect CSS-pixel dimensions and boundaries, then try adjacent targets with a mouse or touch. For cancellation, press and hold, move away, and release using sample data, and verify whether a server-side action occurred. For accessible naming, compare visible text with the computed name and repeat after localization or state changes. Keyboard access is important, but a keyboard-only workaround does not automatically meet a requirement for an alternative operable by a single pointer.
Required practical activity
Use a task board without dragging. Design and test a menu that moves a card between columns with taps.
Knowledge check
What alternative addresses a draggable task card?
Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

lessons.title: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
lessons.objective: Explain WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.

content.text: Learning objectives
Explain WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA), identify the barrier it addresses, and apply and test an appropriate solution.
The accessibility problem

The AA minimum target-size criterion generally requires targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with specified exceptions for spacing, equivalent controls, inline targets, unmodified user-agent controls and essential presentation.
Implementation and testing

For an undersized target, check the actual spacing exception using 24-CSS-pixel diameter circles centered on the target bounds and their relationship to nearby targets. Merely adding a few pixels of margin is not automatically sufficient.
Real-world example: the barrier
Adjacent 16-by-16 CSS pixel icon buttons have no spacing. A user tapping one often activates its neighbor.
Improved design and verification
Increase the target to 24 by 24 CSS pixels or assess the precise spacing exception. Inspect each target and its neighbors, including the specified centered circles.
Implementation demonstration
Problematic approach:
button.icon { width: 16px; height: 16px; } with closely packed neighbors.
Improved approach:
button.icon { min-width: 24px; min-height: 24px; }
If relying on spacing instead of size, evaluate the actual centered 24-pixel circles against nearby targets as specified by the exception.
Detailed guidance

A pointer target is the area that accepts the input, not necessarily the visible icon. A tiny icon can sit inside a larger clickable button, while a large visual graphic can still have an unexpectedly small interactive region. Users with limited accuracy may miss a target or activate its neighbor, especially on touch devices.

The general AA minimum is 24 by 24 CSS pixels. The criterion includes specific exceptions for spacing, equivalent targets, inline targets, unmodified user-agent controls and essential presentation. The spacing exception is precise: center a 24-CSS-pixel-diameter circle on each undersized target bounding box and assess intersections with other targets or the circles of other undersized targets. A vague claim that buttons are “far enough apart” is not a measurement.

The equivalent exception depends on another control on the same page that achieves the same function and meets the criterion. An inline link in a sentence is handled differently because line height can constrain it; this is not permission to shrink every button placed near text. Some presentation is essential or legally required, so examine the actual exception rather than labeling an inconvenient design essential.

Use browser developer tools to measure rendered hit areas in CSS pixels and inspect adjacent controls. Test at several zoom levels and with a touch pointer. For an undersized target, draw or calculate the relevant circles and check each neighboring target. The separate AAA enhanced criterion normally uses 44 by 44 CSS pixels and different exceptions.
Further explanation and testing

A pointer target is the region that responds to a pointer action, not necessarily the visible icon inside it. Small, crowded targets are difficult for users with tremor, limited dexterity, or imprecise touch. The minimum criterion generally uses a 24 by 24 CSS pixel square, subject to specified exceptions. A CSS pixel is a layout unit and should not be assumed to equal a physical display pixel on every screen.

If a target is smaller than the minimum size, the spacing exception can apply when the specified 24-CSS-pixel-diameter circles centered on undersized targets do not intersect another target or the circle of another undersized target. Other exceptions address equivalent controls, inline targets, user-agent control, and essential presentation under their specific conditions. Assess the actual target and its neighbors; a vague claim that there is “enough whitespace” does not demonstrate the spacing rule.

Use browser inspection tools to measure the hit area, then check the nearest neighboring targets and the relevant circles. Increase padding or restructure the layout when controls are crowded, while keeping hit areas from overlapping. Repeat at different viewport sizes and zoom levels. The enhanced AAA target-size criterion generally uses 44 by 44 CSS pixels and has a different set of exceptions, so the minimum spacing rule should not be transferred to it automatically.
Applied review exercise

Review exercise: Two 16-by-16 icon buttons sit directly beside each other. Enlarge their hit areas to at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels or assess the precise spacing exception using centered 24-pixel-diameter circles and neighboring targets. Measure the clickable region rather than the visible icon and ensure that enlarged regions do not overlap. Check inline links and user-agent controls against their actual exception conditions. At AAA the 44-by-44 enhanced target criterion has different requirements and exceptions.
Implementation review

Implementation review: Measure the clickable bounds of an icon button in CSS pixels. If it cannot contain a 24 by 24 CSS pixel square, assess the exact spacing exception by checking the required centered 24-pixel-diameter circle against neighboring targets and circles for other undersized targets. Enlarging padding may be simpler, but verify that hit regions do not overlap. Check inline links, equivalent targets, and other exceptions according to their stated conditions. The AAA target criterion generally uses 44 by 44 and has different exceptions, so passing the minimum rule does not automatically establish the enhanced one.
Worked example and edge cases

Two adjacent icon buttons each have a sixteen-by-sixteen CSS-pixel hit area. Increase each target to contain a 24 by 24 CSS-pixel square, or carefully evaluate an applicable exception such as spacing. Under the spacing exception, examine the specified 24 CSS-pixel circles centered on undersized targets and whether they intersect another target or the relevant circle around another undersized target. Measure actual hit regions rather than icon artwork and repeat after responsive layout changes. Inline links, equivalent controls, user-agent-determined targets, and essential presentation have specific conditions; identify the applicable condition instead of assuming that all small controls are exempt.
Planning a thorough review

Evaluate the pointer task from the user's perspective, from the initial contact through the final result. Identify whether the design requires a path, multiple contact points, dragging, a down-event, precise targeting, or movement of the device. Those are distinct interaction characteristics, and each has its own requirements and exceptions. Check that an alternative completes the same underlying operation, including any selection, confirmation, and error recovery; an alternative that opens a menu but cannot finish the task is incomplete.

Test the actual interactive region rather than only the visible icon. Use browser tools to inspect CSS-pixel dimensions and boundaries, then try adjacent targets with a mouse or touch. For cancellation, press and hold, move away, and release using sample data, and verify whether a server-side action occurred. For accessible naming, compare visible text with the computed name and repeat after localization or state changes. Keyboard access is important, but a keyboard-only workaround does not automatically meet a requirement for an alternative operable by a single pointer.
Required practical activity
Measure adjacent icon buttons. Increase their hit areas or evaluate the spacing exception using the specified circles, then retest touch activation.

Key takeaway
Test the outcome with the relevant input methods and users; a visual change or a single automated test does not by itself establish conformance.

explanations.q1: Provide conventional exit keys and a visible close control; if exiting requires an unusual method, explain it to the user. Test embedded widgets and dialogs as well as the surrounding page.
explanations.q2: Provide a keyboard-operable pause or frequency control near the content. A motion control is not a substitute for evaluating flashing under 2.3.
explanations.q3: Respect reduced-motion preferences where possible and offer a setting when needed. Replace a zooming transition with an immediate state change while retaining the content and controls.
explanations.q4: Place a visible-on-focus skip link early in the page and connect it to the main content. Semantic landmarks and other mechanisms can also help; test the actual focus movement and reading position.
explanations.q5: Prefer descriptive text such as “Read the refund policy”. If the same short label appears in a structured list or table, test that its relevant context is actually associated and announced.
explanations.q6: Account for overlays when scrolling focus into view, for example with suitable scroll padding. Check at zoomed sizes and with keyboard navigation; the criterion addresses the focused component, not just its outline.
explanations.q7: For ordinary buttons, complete the action on release and permit the user to move away before release. Alternatively provide an appropriate undo, an up-event reversal, or meet another specified condition.
explanations.q8: Provide a conventional undo button alongside shake-to-undo and let users turn shake activation off. Test accidental movement and ensure disabling motion does not remove the alternative.
explanations.q9: For sortable cards, add a menu with Move up and Move down actions. For sliders, offer tap controls or a numeric entry where appropriate, while preserving the underlying operation.
